tasks.content: When we build projects in block-based coding programs, the characters and objects we move around are called sprites. A sprite can be a cat, a robot, a car, a fish, or almost anything you can imagine! Each sprite in a project has its own set of code blocks that tell it what to do, so a program can have many sprites, each behaving differently at the same time. Behind the sprites, there is usually a background, sometimes called a stage or a backdrop, which is the picture that fills the space behind everything else, like a beach, a forest, a classroom, or outer space. The background does not move around like a sprite does, but it sets the scene and helps tell the story of what is happening. Think of it like a play at a theater: the sprites are the actors walking around and doing things, and the background is the scenery painted on the wall behind them, showing the audience where the story takes place. Many coding programs let you choose from a library of ready-made sprites and backgrounds, or draw your own! Choosing the right sprite and background helps make a project feel complete and tells a clearer story. For example, a fish sprite makes much more sense swimming in front of an underwater background than in front of a desert background. Today we will practice matching sprites to backgrounds that make sense together, and we will choose a sprite and background for a project we will keep building in future lessons.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Making Sprites Move and Talk
tasks.content: Now that we know what sprites are, let's learn how to make them move and talk using code blocks! Just like we practiced in earlier lessons, motion blocks let a sprite move around the stage, like "move forward," "turn," or "go to a certain spot." But sprites can do more than just move, they can also talk! Special blocks, sometimes called "say" blocks, make a sprite show a speech bubble with words inside, just like a character talking in a comic book. For example, if we want a dog sprite to walk over to a bone and then say "yummy!" we could build a sequence: first, several "move forward" blocks to walk the dog to the bone, and then a "say yummy" block to show the speech bubble. The order still matters here, just like it always has: if we put the "say" block before the movement blocks, the dog would talk before it even reached the bone, which would not make as much sense for our story. We can also make sprites talk for a certain amount of time, using a block like "say hello for 2 seconds," so the speech bubble disappears automatically after a couple of seconds instead of staying on the screen forever. Combining movement and talking blocks lets us build much more interesting and expressive characters, almost like directing a tiny movie! Today we will build a short sequence where a sprite moves to a specific spot and then says something related to what just happened, testing it to make sure the order and timing make sense.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Events: What Makes Code Start?
tasks.content: We learned in Grade 1 that an event is something that happens, like a tap or click, which tells the computer when to start running code. This year, let's dig a little deeper into different kinds of events, because there is more than one way to start code! One common event is clicking or tapping a green flag, which often starts the whole project at once. Another kind of event is tapping directly on a sprite, which might start only that one sprite's code, without affecting any other sprites on the stage. There are also events based on pressing a certain key on the keyboard, like the up arrow key, which might make a sprite jump every time that key is pressed. Some programs even have events based on one sprite bumping into another sprite, or a sound reaching a certain loudness! Each of these events acts like a trigger, or a starting signal, for a specific set of code blocks. This means one single project can have many different events, each one starting a different action. For example, imagine a game where tapping the green flag starts the background music, tapping a cat sprite makes it meow, and pressing the space bar makes a ball bounce. All three of these are happening in the very same project, but each one is triggered by a different event! Today we will explore several different types of events, and we will match each event to the action it would most likely trigger in a simple example project.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Now it's time to use everything we've learned about sprites, backgrounds, motion, talking, and events to build something wonderful: a simple coded story! A coded story uses sprites as characters, a background as the setting, and sequences of blocks to make the story happen, step by step, just like the stories we read in books, except this time, we are the author and the coder! To plan our story, we first think about the basic parts every story needs: Who are the characters, or sprites? Where does the story happen, or what is the background? What happens first, next, and last? For example, imagine a short story about a turtle who is late for school. We might choose a turtle sprite and a park background. The story could begin with an event, like tapping the green flag, and then the turtle sprite could say "Oh no, I'm late!" using a say block, followed by several "move forward" blocks to show the turtle hurrying across the screen, and finally another say block where the turtle says "I made it!" once it reaches the school. We might even add a loop to make the turtle's legs appear to move quickly as it hurries along. Just like real authors, we can revise our story if something is not working quite right, moving blocks around or adding new ones until the story flows the way we want. Today we will plan a short story with at least one sprite, one background, and at least three events or actions, and then we will build it using blocks, testing it to make sure it tells our story clearly.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: What an incredible year of coding! You have learned so much: reviewing sequences, understanding commands and actions, using repeat loops, exploring loops within loops, debugging loop mistakes, working with sprites and backgrounds, making sprites move and talk, understanding different kinds of events, and even building your very own coded story. Today, we bring everything together in a special mini project that shows off everything you have learned this year. Your task is to build a short interactive scene using sprites, a background, at least one loop, and at least one event. Start by planning: choose your sprite or sprites, choose a background that fits your idea, and sketch out what will happen, step by step, on paper first. Think about which event will start your project, like tapping the green flag or tapping a sprite. Then think about where a loop could make your project better, maybe a character that spins around several times, or bounces up and down a few times in a row. As you build your project with blocks, remember to test it often, running it after adding just a few blocks instead of waiting until the very end. If something does not work the way you expected, use your debugging skills: check the order of your blocks, check the numbers in your loops, and check that each block is doing exactly what you think it should be doing. Once your project works the way you want, share it with a partner, and take turns exploring what you each built. You have grown so much as a coder this year, and you are ready for even bigger challenges next year!
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Multiplayer Basics: Two Sprites, Two Players

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Multiplayer Basics: Two Sprites, Two Players
tasks.content: A simple two-player game can use two sprites, each controlled by different keys - like arrow keys for one player and W/A/S/D for the other. Each sprite needs its own movement code listening for its own set of keys, and the game might check for a winner, like which sprite reaches a goal first or collects more points.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: In a two-player game, how are the two sprites typically controlled?
options: By the exact same single key

questions.questionText: Give an example of a key set one player might use, besides arrow keys.
What does each sprite need, to respond to its own player's keys?
questions.correctAnswer: Its own movement code listening for its own keys
options: Its own movement code listening for its own keys
The exact same code as the other sprite

questions.questionText: What might a two-player game check for, to determine the outcome?
questions.correctAnswer: a winner (e.g. who reaches a goal first or scores more points)

questions.questionText: Why does each sprite need separate key-listening code in a two-player game?
questions.correctAnswer: So each player's input only controls their own sprite

Separate code has no purpose in multiplayer games
Only one sprite can ever be controlled at a time

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Introduction to Variables in Scratch
tasks.content: A variable in Scratch is a labelled storage box that holds a value, which you can create, change, and display on the screen - like a variable called 'points' that starts at 0 and increases every time something happens in your game. Variables let your program remember and update information as it runs.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What is a variable in Scratch?
questions.correctAnswer: A labelled storage box that holds a value
options: A labelled storage box that holds a value
A fixed value that can never be created or changed

questions.questionText: What example variable is given in the lesson, which might start at 0?

questions.correctAnswer: remember and update information as it runs

questions.questionText: Can a variable's value be displayed on the screen?
options: Only if the computer is restarted

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why is a variable described as a 'labelled' storage box, rather than just a storage box?
questions.correctAnswer: the label (name) tells you and the program what specific piece of information that box is storing

questions.questionText: Why might a game need a variable to track 'points', rather than just hardcoding a fixed score into the program?

options: A variable can change as the game is played, accurately reflecting the player's current progress, unlike a fixed number
A fixed, hardcoded number works exactly the same as using a variable

questions.questionText: Why might displaying a variable's value on the screen be useful for a player of a game?

questions.questionText: Why are variables considered an essential concept for building almost any interactive Scratch project?

options: Most interactive projects need to track changing information, like scores, lives or time, which variables are designed to store
Variables have no real use in most interactive Scratch projects

tasks.content: Scratch's music blocks let you play notes, choose instruments, and set tempo (speed) to create your own simple tunes or sound effects. Combining a sequence of 'play note' blocks, each with a specific pitch and duration, lets you compose a short melody that plays when your project starts or a sprite is clicked.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: Why might changing the tempo of a melody change how a piece of music feels, even with the same notes?

tasks.content: Skimming means reading a text quickly to get a general idea of what it is about, often by glancing at titles, headings and first sentences rather than every word. Scanning means moving your eyes quickly over a text to find a specific piece of information, like a date, name or number, without reading everything in between. Both strategies help you find information quickly, instead of reading a whole text word by word.
Let's practice what we just learned!

scan for key words or numbers

options: Running your eyes down the page looking for a specific word

questions.correctAnswer: get a quick overview before reading in detail

tasks.content: A noun phrase can be expanded by adding extra words that describe it in more detail, making writing far more interesting to read. You can add more than one adjective before the noun, like 'the enormous, shaggy dog', or add a phrase after it using a preposition, like 'the dog with muddy paws'. Expanding noun phrases helps the reader picture exactly what you mean, rather than a vague image.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: Which is an expanded noun phrase?

questions.correctAnswer: The cat with the torn ear slept on the mat.

options: To add extra descriptive detail to a noun

tasks.content: A fronted adverbial is a word or phrase placed at the start of a sentence, before the main clause, to tell the reader when, where or how something happens. A comma always follows a fronted adverbial, for example 'Later that day, we went to the beach' or 'Without warning, the alarm rang.' Fronted adverbials add variety to your sentences and help control the pace and order of your writing.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: Which sentence has a fronted adverbial?
questions.correctAnswer: Later, we went to the park.
options: We went to the park later.

tasks.content: Cohesion means ideas connect smoothly and logically, both within and between paragraphs. Writers link paragraphs using connecting phrases such as 'however', 'in addition' or 'as a result', by repeating key words, or by using pronouns like 'it' or 'they' to refer back to something mentioned earlier. Without these links, writing can feel like a list of unrelated ideas rather than a flowing piece.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Standard English is the form of English with agreed grammar rules, generally used in formal writing and speech, such as 'I did it' rather than 'I done it', or 'We were happy' rather than 'We was happy'. Informal, spoken English can include regional dialect words and grammar that don't follow these rules, which is fine in casual conversation, but formal writing — like a letter or a report — usually needs Standard English.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Persuasive writing uses language deliberately to convince a reader to agree with a viewpoint. Writers use emotive language, choosing words that stir up feelings, such as 'desperately' or 'heartbreaking'. They also use rhetorical questions, which make the reader think and agree without expecting a real answer, and they often speak directly to the reader using 'you' to make the argument feel personal.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses emotive language to persuade?

options: These poor, abandoned dogs desperately need your help.

questions.correctAnswer: To make the reader think and agree without expecting a reply
options: To get an actual spoken answer
To make the reader think and agree without expecting a reply

tasks.content: An explanation text answers 'how' and 'why' questions, describing a process clearly and often in the present tense, for example how volcanoes erupt or why leaves change colour. Explanation texts use causal connectives such as 'this causes', 'as a result' and 'because', and often include diagrams to show a process visually. This makes them different from instructions, which tell the reader what to do step by step.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Possessive pronouns such as 'mine', 'yours', 'his', 'hers', 'its', 'ours' and 'theirs' show that something belongs to someone, and importantly, they never use an apostrophe. tasks.content: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as', such as 'as brave as a lion' or 'the water sparkled like diamonds'. A metaphor compares two things by saying one thing IS another, without using 'like' or 'as' - such as 'the classroom was a zoo'. tasks.content: Column addition and subtraction line numbers up by place value - ones under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds - so we can add or subtract each column in turn. In addition, if a column adds up to 10 or more, we carry the extra ten into the next column. In subtraction, if the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit, we exchange (borrow) 10 from the column to its left. Setting work out neatly in columns helps avoid mistakes with bigger numbers.

tasks.content: ஆத்திசூடி (Aathichudi) is one of the most famous books ever written for Tamil children. It was written long ago by the poet ஔவையார் (Auvaiyar), and it is a list of short, one-line sayings that each teach a good habit or a good value. The clever part is that the sayings are arranged in the order of the Tamil alphabet — the first saying starts with அ, the second with ஆ, the third with இ, and so on! This helped children learn their letters and good manners at the same time. Here are some famous lines: "அறம் செய விரும்பு" means "Wish to do good deeds." "ஆறுவது சினம்" means "Let your anger cool down" — it reminds us not to stay angry. "ஈவது விலக்கேல்" means "Do not stop someone from giving to others." tasks.content: The human digestive system breaks down the food we eat so our bodies can use it for energy and growth. Food travels from the mouth, where teeth chew it and saliva begins breaking it down, down a tube called the oesophagus into the stomach, where powerful acids and muscles churn it into a soupy mixture. It then passes into the small intestine, where nutrients are absorbed into the blood, before moving to the large intestine, which absorbs water, and finally leftover waste leaves the body.

tasks.content: All materials exist in one of three states: solid, liquid, or gas. Solids, like an ice cube, have a fixed shape and volume, while liquids, like water, take the shape of their container but keep the same volume, and gases, like steam, spread out to fill whatever space they are in. Many materials can change between these states when heated or cooled; for example, ice melts into liquid water at 0 degrees Celsius, and water boils into steam, a gas, at 100 degrees Celsius.

tasks.content: All sounds are made when something vibrates, meaning it moves rapidly back and forth, such as a guitar string or your vocal cords when you speak. These vibrations travel outward through a medium, like air or water, as sound waves that eventually reach our ears, letting us hear the sound. The pitch of a sound, whether it is high or low, depends on how fast the object vibrates; a short, tight guitar string vibrates quickly and makes a high pitch, while a long, loose string vibrates slowly and makes a low pitch.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A simple electrical circuit needs a complete, unbroken loop of wires connecting a power source, like a battery, to a component such as a bulb, buzzer, or motor, often with a switch to turn it on and off. If there is a gap anywhere in the circuit, such as an open switch, electricity cannot flow and the bulb will not light up. Materials that let electricity flow through them easily, like metals such as copper, are called conductors, while materials that do not, like plastic or rubber, are called insulators.

tasks.content: Environments are always at risk of changing, sometimes due to natural events like drought or flooding, and sometimes because of human actions like cutting down forests or polluting rivers, which can be dangerous for the living things that depend on that habitat. When an environment changes, it can affect a whole food chain; for example, if a drought kills off grass, the animals that eat the grass may struggle to survive, which then affects the predators that eat those animals. Understanding food chains, with producers, predators, and prey, helps us see how connected living things really are.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Humans and many animals have different types of teeth, each shaped for a different job in eating. Incisors are the flat, sharp teeth at the front of the mouth used for biting and cutting food, canines are the pointed teeth used for tearing tougher food, and molars are the large, flat teeth at the back of the mouth used for grinding and chewing food into smaller pieces. Carnivores, like lions, tend to have large, sharp canines for tearing meat, while herbivores, like cows, have large flat molars suited to grinding tough plants.

tasks.content: The water cycle describes how water moves continuously between the Earth's surface and the sky. The sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes, causing it to evaporate, meaning it turns from a liquid into water vapour, a gas, and rises into the air. As this water vapour rises and cools, it condenses back into tiny liquid droplets, forming clouds, and when the droplets become heavy enough, they fall back to the ground as precipitation, such as rain or snow, before flowing back into rivers and seas to begin the cycle again.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Once scientists carry out a test, they need to gather and record their data carefully so nothing is forgotten and the results can be understood clearly. This often means taking accurate measurements, using equipment such as a ruler, thermometer, or measuring jug, and writing the numbers down straight away in an organised table. Recording data in a table, and sometimes presenting it in a bar chart, makes it much easier to compare results and spot patterns, such as noticing that plants grown in sunlight grew taller than plants grown in the dark.

tasks.content: Selection is a way of making a program choose between different actions, depending on whether something is true or false. It uses a special block or instruction called if, which checks a condition, and only runs the blocks inside it if that condition is true. For example, an if block might say: if the character touches the edge, then turn around. This means the turning instruction only happens when the character is actually touching the edge, and is skipped completely the rest of the time. Selection often uses an extra part called else, which tells the program what to do instead, if the condition is false. For example: if the score is greater than 10, then say you win, else say try again. This means the program checks the score, and picks one of the two messages depending on whether the condition is true or false, but never both. Selection is different from sequence, because a sequence always runs every instruction, while selection only runs certain instructions when a condition is met. Selection lets programs react differently in different situations, which makes games and programs feel much more interesting and lifelike, because they can respond sensibly to what is actually happening.

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Variables: Storing Information in Programs
tasks.content: A variable is a named place in a program where we can store a piece of information, such as a number or some text, so the program can use it and change it while it runs. Think of a variable as a labelled box. We give the box a sensible name, like score or player name, and we can put a value inside it, look at what is inside it, or change what is inside it, as the program runs. For example, a program might create a variable called score, set it to 0 at the start, and then add 1 to it every time the player collects a coin. Later, the program can check the value stored in score to decide what to display, such as showing you win if the score reaches 10. Variables are useful because they let a program remember information between different parts of the program, rather than forgetting it straight away. Without variables, a program could not keep track of a score, remember a player's name, or count how many lives are left. Choosing clear, sensible names for variables, such as score rather than a single confusing letter, makes programs much easier to read, understand, and debug later on.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Designing a Program: Planning Before Coding

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Designing a Program: Planning Before Coding
tasks.content: Before writing a program, it is very helpful to plan it carefully, rather than jumping straight into coding. Planning helps us think clearly about what the program needs to do, and it often saves time later by avoiding mistakes and confusion. One useful way to plan is to write down the program's purpose in a single clear sentence, such as this program will let the player move a character to collect stars. Next, we can list the main steps or events needed, such as what happens when the program starts, what happens when a key is pressed, and what happens when the character touches a star. Many programmers also sketch a simple diagram or storyboard, which shows what the program's screen should look like at different points, helping us picture the finished program before building it. Planning also involves thinking about what inputs the program needs, such as key presses or mouse clicks, and what outputs it should produce, such as sounds, messages, or a changing score. Taking time to plan does not mean the design cannot change once we start coding, because new ideas often appear while building a program, but having a clear plan gives us a strong, sensible starting point and makes debugging much easier later on.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Decomposition means breaking a large, complicated problem down into smaller, more manageable parts, so that it becomes much easier to understand and solve. This is an important skill in computing, because trying to solve a big problem all at once can feel overwhelming and confusing, but solving several small, clear parts is usually much simpler. For example, imagine we want to create a program for a simple quiz game. Instead of trying to build the whole thing at once, we could break it down into smaller parts, such as showing a question, checking the player's answer, keeping score, and showing a final result. Each of these smaller parts can be planned and built separately, and then combined together to make the whole program work. Decomposition is not just used in computing. We use it in everyday life too, such as breaking down the big task of tidying a bedroom into smaller jobs, like putting away clothes, tidying the desk, and making the bed. Breaking a problem down also makes it much easier to find and fix bugs, because if something goes wrong, we can check each small part on its own, rather than searching through one enormous, complicated program all at once.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A spreadsheet is a computer program used to organise, calculate, and display information using rows and columns, forming a grid of boxes called cells. Each cell can hold different types of information, such as a word, a number, or a formula, and each cell has its own address, made from a column letter and a row number, such as B3, which means column B, row 3. Spreadsheets are extremely useful for organising lists of information, such as a list of pupils' names alongside their scores in a spelling test. One of the most powerful features of spreadsheets is the ability to use formulas, which are special instructions that automatically calculate a result using the values in other cells. For example, a formula could automatically add up all the numbers in a column to find a total, or work out an average score, and if any of the numbers change, the formula updates the answer automatically, without us needing to recalculate it by hand. Spreadsheets can also create charts and graphs from our data, which helps us see patterns more easily than looking at rows of numbers alone. Learning to use spreadsheets helps us organise information clearly and carry out calculations quickly and accurately.

levels.levelName: How the Internet Works: An Overview

tasks.taskName: Lesson: How the Internet Works: An Overview
tasks.content: The internet is a huge, worldwide network that connects billions of computers and devices together, allowing them to share information almost instantly. When we use the internet, our device does not usually talk directly to the website we want. Instead, our request travels through many connected devices and cables, including underwater cables that stretch between countries, and wireless signals, until it reaches the computer that stores the website we asked for, known as a server. A server is simply a powerful computer that stores information and sends it out whenever it is requested, so that other computers, called clients, can access it. When we type a website address, our device sends a request across the network to find the correct server, and the server sends back the information needed to show the webpage on our screen, all usually within a fraction of a second. Every device connected to the internet has its own address, called an IP address, a bit like a postal address, which helps information find its way to exactly the right place. Understanding that the internet is made of real physical cables, wireless signals, servers, and addresses helps us see it as a vast, organised system, rather than something magical or invisible.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Evaluating Websites: Is It True?
tasks.content: Not everything found on the internet is accurate, up to date, or true, so it is an important skill to be able to evaluate a website, which means judging carefully whether we should trust the information on it. One helpful thing to check is who wrote or published the website, because information from a well-known, trusted organisation, such as a museum, a government website, or a respected news source, is usually more reliable than a website with no named author at all. It is also helpful to check when a website was last updated, because some information, especially facts about current events or fast-changing topics, can quickly become out of date. Another useful strategy is to compare the same piece of information across two or three different trusted websites, because if several reliable sources agree, the information is more likely to be accurate. We should also be alert to websites that seem to be trying to sell us something, or that use exaggerated claims and dramatic language, because this can be a sign that the information is biased or not entirely truthful. If we are ever unsure whether a website can be trusted, the best thing to do is ask a trusted adult or teacher, who can help us decide together whether the information is reliable.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A digital footprint is the trail of information left behind by everything we do online, such as messages we send, photographs we post, comments we make, and websites we visit. Just like footprints left in sand can show where someone has walked, our digital footprint can show what we have done and said on the internet, and importantly, this trail can sometimes be seen by other people, and can be very difficult to completely remove once it exists. It is important to think carefully before posting or sharing anything online, because even things that feel private at the time, such as a photograph shared with what seems like only a few friends, could potentially be copied, shared further, or seen by people we did not expect. A helpful habit is to pause and think before posting, and ask ourselves whether we would be comfortable with a trusted adult, a teacher, or even a future employer seeing it one day. We should never post personal details, such as our address or school, and we should always ask a trusted adult before sharing photographs or videos of ourselves online. Being thoughtful about our digital footprint now helps protect our privacy and reputation, both today and in the future.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Animation is the process of making still pictures appear to move, by showing a fast sequence of slightly different images, one after another. This works because our eyes and brain blend the quick series of images together, creating the illusion of smooth movement, a trick that has been used in cartoons and films for many years. In digital animation, we often build this effect using frames, where each frame is a single image, and playing many frames quickly, one after another, makes the animation appear to move smoothly. In simple block-based coding, we can create animation using costumes, which are different versions of a character, and switching between costumes quickly using a loop can make a character appear to walk, jump, or flap its wings. For example, a program might say: repeat 10 times: switch to next costume, wait a fraction of a second. Another common animation technique is changing a character's position slightly, over and over again, in a loop, to make it appear to glide smoothly across the screen. Good animation usually needs small, careful changes between each frame or costume, because if the change between images is too large, the movement can look jumpy rather than smooth. Planning an animation, such as sketching the key positions first, helps make the final movement look believable.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Combining Software Tools for a Project
tasks.content: Many real projects on a computer are made by combining several different software tools together, rather than using just one program on its own. For example, imagine creating a project about the water cycle for the whole class to see. We might use a drawing program to create pictures of clouds, rain, and rivers, a word processing program to write clear explanations, and a slideshow program to bring the pictures and writing together into an organised, easy to follow presentation. Combining tools like this lets us use each program for the job it does best, such as using a drawing tool for illustrations and a word processor for detailed writing, rather than trying to force one single program to do every single job. When combining tools, it is important to plan first, deciding what each part of the finished project will need, such as which pictures are required, how much text each slide should have, and in what order everything should appear. It also helps to keep our files organised in clearly named folders, so we can find the pictures, documents, and slides easily when we need to bring them all together. Learning to combine software tools thoughtfully helps us create polished, well-organised projects that communicate our ideas clearly and effectively.

levels.levelName: The Scratch Interface: Stage, Sprites, Blocks

tasks.taskName: Lesson: The Scratch Interface: Stage, Sprites, Blocks
tasks.content: This year, we are moving up to a real, powerful coding program used by millions of kids around the world: Scratch! Scratch was created to help young people learn to code by snapping together colorful blocks, and today we will explore its main parts. The first important part is the stage, which is the rectangle in the corner of the screen where your project actually plays, showing the sprites, the background, and any action happening. Next are sprites, the characters or objects in your project, like a cat, a dragon, or a basketball, each one able to move, talk, and follow its own code. Every sprite you add appears in the sprite list, usually below the stage, where you can click on any sprite to work on its code. The last major part is the blocks palette, found on the left side of the screen, which holds every single block you could possibly use, organized into colorful categories like Motion, which is blue, Looks, which is purple, Sound, which is a pinkish color, Events, which is yellow, Control, which is orange, and more. To build a program, you drag blocks from the palette into the large white coding area in the middle of the screen, snapping them together like puzzle pieces to build a sequence. Learning where everything lives in Scratch, the stage, the sprite list, the blocks palette, and the coding area, will make everything else we learn this year much easier. Today we will take a guided tour of the Scratch interface, clicking on different parts and predicting what each one is used for before we try it ourselves.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Motion Blocks: Making Sprites Move
tasks.content: Motion blocks are the blue blocks in Scratch, and they control everything about how a sprite moves and where it faces. Some of the most common motion blocks include "move 10 steps," which moves a sprite forward in the direction it is currently facing, "turn right 15 degrees" and "turn left 15 degrees," which rotate the sprite, and "go to x: 0 y: 0," which instantly teleports a sprite to a specific spot on the stage. Scratch uses a coordinate system to describe exact positions on the stage, using two numbers called x and y. The x number tells how far left or right a sprite is, and the y number tells how far up or down it is, with the very center of the stage being x: 0, y: 0. Understanding coordinates helps us place sprites exactly where we want them, instead of just guessing. Another useful motion block is "glide 1 second to x: ___ y: ___," which moves a sprite smoothly to a new spot over time, instead of jumping there instantly, which can make animations look much more natural. If a sprite ever points in a direction that seems upside down or sideways after turning, we can use the "point in direction" block to fix it and set it facing exactly the way we want. Motion blocks are often combined with loops, letting a sprite move forward repeatedly to travel a long distance, or bounce back and forth across the stage. Today we will experiment with different motion blocks, testing how numbers change a sprite's movement, and we will use coordinates to guide a sprite to a specific target spot on the stage.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Loop Blocks: Repeat and Forever
tasks.content: In Scratch, loop blocks live in the orange Control category, and they help us repeat actions without writing the same blocks again and again. We already know about the repeat block, which repeats whatever blocks are snapped inside it a certain number of times, like "repeat 10." But Scratch also has another very important loop called the forever block, which repeats whatever is inside it endlessly, without ever stopping on its own, until the project is stopped completely. The forever block is extremely useful for things that should always be happening, like a sprite that should always follow the mouse pointer around the stage, or a background that should always slowly change color throughout the entire project. However, we need to be careful with forever blocks, because anything placed after a forever block in a sequence will actually never run, since the forever loop never finishes on its own to let the program continue! This is different from a repeat block, which does eventually finish after its set number of repeats, allowing the program to continue on to whatever comes next. Choosing between repeat and forever depends entirely on what we want our project to do. If we want an action to happen an exact number of times, like a character taking exactly five steps, we use repeat. If we want something to keep happening for as long as the project is running, like a spinning windmill in the background, we use forever. Today we will experiment with both repeat and forever blocks, comparing what happens when we place blocks after each one, and we will decide which loop fits different project ideas best.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Event Blocks: When Green Flag Clicked

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Event Blocks: When Green Flag Clicked
tasks.content: Event blocks in Scratch are yellow, hat-shaped blocks that sit at the very top of a sequence, and they decide exactly when the blocks underneath them will start running. The most common event block in Scratch is "when green flag clicked," which starts the attached code the moment someone clicks the green flag icon above the stage, which is how almost every Scratch project begins. Another important event block is "when this sprite clicked," which only runs its code when someone clicks directly on that particular sprite, not the whole project. Scratch also has "when key pressed," which lets us choose a specific keyboard key, like the space bar or an arrow key, so the code underneath only runs when that exact key is pressed. There is also a broadcast-related event, "when I receive," which we will learn much more about very soon, that starts code when a message is sent from somewhere else in the project. Every single script, which is what we call a connected stack of blocks, needs an event block at the top, or it will never run at all, no matter how perfectly the rest of the blocks are built! This is an important rule to remember: without an event, blocks just sit in the coding area, doing nothing. A single Scratch project can, and usually does, have many different scripts, each starting with its own event block, allowing many different things to happen depending on what the person playing the project actually does. Today we will build several small scripts, each starting with a different event block, and test how each one behaves differently.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Sound blocks in Scratch are a pinkish-magenta color, and they let us add music, sound effects, and audio to our projects, making them feel much more exciting and alive. One common sound block is "play sound until done," which plays a chosen sound and waits for it to completely finish before moving on to the next block in the script. There is also "start sound," which plays a sound but does not wait, letting the rest of the script keep running at the very same time as the sound plays, which is useful when you want a sprite to move and make noise simultaneously. Scratch comes with a large sound library full of ready-made sound effects, like a pop, a meow, or drum beats, and you can also record your own sounds using a microphone, or upload sound files from your computer! Sound blocks also let us adjust volume, using a block like "change volume by," and we can even add fun effects, like "set pitch effect," which can make a sound sound higher or lower, almost like a cartoon character's voice. Adding well-chosen sound to a project can completely change how it feels: imagine a spooky Halloween scene with eerie sound effects, compared to the very same scene with cheerful, bouncy music instead, it would feel like a totally different project! It is important to choose sounds that match the mood and story of your project, rather than just picking random sounds. Today we will explore the built-in sound library, test the difference between "play sound until done" and "start sound," and add at least one sound effect to a sprite's script.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: So far, every script we have built runs the exact same way every single time. But real programs, like games, often need to make decisions, doing different things depending on what is happening. That is where the if-then block comes in! The if-then block is found in the Control category, and it checks whether something is true or false. If the condition inside the block is true, the blocks snapped inside it will run. If the condition is false, those blocks are simply skipped, and the script continues on without them. For example, imagine a game where a cat sprite should say "You found it!" only if it touches a treasure sprite. We could build this using an if-then block: "if touching treasure, then say You found it!" If the cat is not touching the treasure, nothing happens, the cat stays quiet, and the game keeps going normally. The condition inside an if-then block often uses special blocks shaped like hexagons, like "touching \_\_?" or "key pressed?", which return either true or false depending on what is currently happening in the project. If-then blocks are usually placed inside a forever loop, so the computer keeps checking the condition over and over again, watching for exactly the right moment for it to become true, like constantly checking whether the cat has touched the treasure yet. Making decisions with if-then blocks is a huge step up from everything we have learned so far, because it lets our projects respond differently depending on what is actually happening, instead of always doing the exact same thing. Today we will build a script using an if-then block inside a forever loop, testing what happens when the condition is true compared to when it is false.
Let's practice what we just learned!

options: It runs certain blocks only if a condition is true; otherwise it skips them

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Introduction to Variables: Keeping Score
tasks.content: A variable is like a labeled box that stores a piece of information a program needs to remember and can change over time. In Scratch, variables show up as orange blocks, and one of the most common uses for a variable is keeping score in a game! Let's say we want to build a simple game where a sprite earns a point every time it touches a coin sprite. First, we would create a variable, maybe named "score," and set it to 0 at the very beginning of the game, using a "set score to 0" block. Then, inside an if-then block that checks whether the sprite is touching the coin, we would add a "change score by 1" block, which adds one point to the score every single time the condition becomes true. Scratch can even show the current value of a variable right on the stage, like a little scoreboard in the corner, which updates automatically every time the variable changes, without us needing to do anything extra. Variables are not just for scores, they can store all kinds of information a program needs to remember, like a player's name, the number of lives left, or how much time is remaining. The important thing to understand about a variable is that its value can change while the program is running, unlike a fixed number that always stays the same. This is what makes variables so powerful: they let our projects remember and react to what has happened so far. Today we will create a score variable, set it to 0 at the start, and use a "change score by 1" block combined with an if-then block to build a very simple point-scoring game.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Now that our Scratch projects are getting more complex, with motion, loops, events, sounds, if-then blocks, and variables all working together, debugging becomes even more important, and even more interesting! When a Scratch project does not behave the way we expect, there are several strategies we can use to find the problem. First, we can click on individual blocks, or small groups of blocks, directly in the coding area, which runs just that part of the script by itself, helping us narrow down exactly where the problem might be hiding. Second, we can check our event blocks: is there an event block at the top of every script, and is it the right kind of event? Third, we can look closely at any if-then blocks: is the condition actually checking the right thing, like the correct sprite name or the correct variable? Fourth, we can watch variables on the stage while the project runs, checking whether they are changing the way we expect, like whether a score variable is actually going up when it should. A very common Scratch bug happens when a forever loop is missing, causing an if-then block to only check its condition one single time instead of continuously watching for it. Another common bug happens when blocks are snapped to the wrong sprite's script instead of the sprite we intended. Debugging in Scratch is a lot like being a detective: we gather clues, like what we expected to happen compared to what actually happened, and we test small changes one at a time, instead of changing many things at once, which can make it confusing to tell what actually fixed the problem. Today we will debug several sample projects with common Scratch mistakes already built in, working through each one using the strategies from this lesson.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: It's time to bring together everything we have learned this year, motion, loops, events, sound, if-then blocks, and variables, to design our very own simple game in Scratch! Designing a game starts with an idea, not with blocks. Before opening Scratch, good game designers think through some important questions: What is the goal of the game? How does the player control what happens? What makes the player win, or lose? For example, let's design a simple catching game: a basket sprite moves left and right using arrow key events, while an apple sprite falls from the top of the stage using motion blocks inside a loop. If the apple touches the basket, we use an if-then block to increase a score variable and reset the apple back to the top. If the apple reaches the bottom of the stage without touching the basket, the game could end, or a lives variable could go down by one instead. Notice how this one simple game idea actually uses almost everything we learned this year: events to control the basket, loops to keep the apple falling and the game running, if-then blocks to check for touching, and variables to track score. When designing your own game, it helps to start simple, get one basic part working first, like making the apple fall, before adding more complicated parts, like scoring and losing. This is exactly how professional game designers work too, building and testing one piece at a time instead of trying to build the whole game all at once. Today we will sketch a simple game idea on paper, listing which Scratch blocks we think we will need, before starting to build it step by step in Scratch.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: What a huge year of learning! You explored the Scratch interface, used motion blocks to move sprites, learned the difference between repeat and forever loops, used event blocks to control when scripts start, added sound and music to your projects, made decisions with if-then blocks, tracked information with variables, practiced debugging Scratch projects, and even designed your own simple game. Today's mini project is your chance to show off everything you have learned by building a complete small game or interactive project from start to finish. Begin with planning: sketch your idea on paper first, deciding on your sprites, your background, your goal, and how the player will control what happens. Think carefully about which events will start different parts of your project, whether you need a repeat loop or a forever loop, where an if-then block could check for something important, like touching another sprite, and whether a variable, like a score or a counter, would make your project more interesting. As you build, remember the debugging strategies we practiced: test small pieces as you go instead of waiting until the very end, click on small groups of blocks to check exactly what they do, and watch your variables while the project runs to make sure they behave the way you expect. If something is not working, take a breath, think like a detective, and look for clues about what is actually happening compared to what you expected. Once your project works, share it with a partner or the class, and try out a few other classmates' projects too, noticing how everyone combined the very same tools, motion, loops, events, sound, if-then blocks, and variables, in completely different and creative ways. You are becoming real Scratch programmers, and next year we will go even further with your skills!
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A nested loop is a loop placed inside another loop, useful for repeating a pattern of actions multiple times. For example, 'repeat 3 times: [repeat 4 times: move forward, turn right]' could draw a more complex shape than a single loop alone. Nested loops let you build more complex, structured patterns of repetition in your programs.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A broadcast is a message one sprite (character) sends that other sprites can 'hear' and react to, letting them communicate and coordinate. tasks.content: Broadcast and receive blocks let different sprites communicate with each other: one sprite can 'broadcast' a message, and any sprite with a matching 'when I receive' block will respond, even without being directly connected. tasks.content: A nested loop is a loop placed inside another loop, letting you repeat a repeated action - like a loop that draws a square (4 sides) nested inside another loop that repeats the whole square 6 times to create a pattern of squares. Nested loops are a powerful way to create complex repeating patterns from simple building blocks.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.correctAnswer: Complex repeating patterns from simple building blocks
options: Complex repeating patterns from simple building blocks

options: Only a single action, with no repetition

tasks.content: A theme is an underlying idea or message running through a text, such as courage, loss or friendship. When comparing two texts that share a theme, look at how each writer's choices — their language, characters, tone and structure — shape a different treatment of that same idea. One story about facing fears might end triumphantly, while another ends more thoughtfully, showing that authors can approach the same theme in very different ways.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A relative clause adds extra information about a noun, and begins with a relative pronoun: 'who' for people, 'which' for things, 'where' for places, 'whose' for possession, and 'that' for people or things. For example, 'The girl who won the race is my sister' or 'The house, which was built in 1900, is for sale.' Relative clauses let you combine two ideas into one detailed sentence.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Modal verbs go before another verb to show how possible, certain or necessary something is. 'Might' and 'could' show something is only possible, 'should' can show advice or likelihood, and 'must' shows strong certainty or obligation. Choosing a different modal verb changes how confident a sentence sounds: compare 'It might rain' with 'It must rain' — the second sounds far more certain.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Across a whole text, not just within one paragraph, writers use cohesion devices to keep ideas connected. Pronouns like 'it', 'this' and 'they' refer back to something mentioned earlier, avoiding repetition, while adverbials such as 'consequently' or 'nevertheless' link paragraphs together by showing a result or a contrast. Deliberately repeating a key word can also remind the reader of the main idea running through a text.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Parenthesis is extra, non-essential information inserted into the middle of a sentence, marked off with a pair of commas, brackets, or dashes, for example 'My brother, who is ten, loves football' or 'The trip (which cost £50) was worth it.' tasks.content: A discussion text presents both sides of an argument fairly, often organised into a section 'for' one view and a section 'for' the other, before ending with a balanced conclusion. Pathetic fallacy — using weather or setting to reflect a character's emotions, like a storm during a frightening scene — is another powerful way to build suspense.

tasks.content: Register means how formal or informal a piece of writing is, and choosing the right register depends on your audience and purpose. Formal writing avoids contractions and slang, uses full sentences and a polite, objective tone, and suits letters to people you don't know or official reports. Informal writing uses contractions, casual phrases and sometimes slang, and suits texting a friend.

tasks.content: Etymology is the study of where words come from, and many English words originate from Latin and Greek. Knowing common roots helps you work out the meaning and spelling of unfamiliar words: the Greek root 'tele' means 'far', as in 'telephone' and 'television', while the Latin prefix 'bi-' means 'two', as in 'bicycle'. Spotting these patterns turns spelling into detective work rather than guesswork.

tasks.content: Formal writing uses full words (not contractions), avoids slang, and keeps a serious, polite tone - used for things like letters to a headteacher or school reports. Informal writing is more relaxed, can use contractions like 'don't' and 'it's', and sounds more like everyday speech - used for texts to friends or diary entries. Choosing the right style depends on who you're writing to and why.

tasks.content: Standard English follows the accepted rules of grammar and is used in formal situations, like school writing or official letters, while informal language is more relaxed and used with friends or family, often including slang or contractions. Knowing when to use each is an important writing skill - you wouldn't write 'gonna' in a formal letter, but it might be fine in a text to a friend.

tasks.content: A balanced argument presents both sides of an issue fairly, giving reasons for each viewpoint before reaching a conclusion, unlike a persuasive piece that only argues for one side. tasks.content: Numbers up to a million are built from millions, hundred-thousands, ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. tasks.content: When you multiply a number by 10, every digit moves one place to the left, which looks like adding a zero for whole numbers - 24 x 10 = 240. Multiplying by 100 moves digits two places left, and by 1,000 moves them three places left. Dividing works the opposite way: digits move to the right, so 240 / 10 = 24 and 2400 / 100 = 24. Remember, the digits move, not just the decimal point being 'added'.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Rounding makes numbers simpler while keeping them close to their real value - useful for checking if an answer is sensible. To round to the nearest 10, look at the ones digit: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down, so 47 rounds to 50 and 43 rounds to 40. The same rule applies for rounding to the nearest 100 or 1,000, just look at the next digit down. Estimating means rounding numbers first to make a calculation quicker, like estimating 198 + 303 as 200 + 300 = 500.

To find the area of a rectangle, multiply its length by its width: a rectangle 5 cm long and 3 cm wide has an area of 5 x 3 = 15 cm2. Unlike perimeter (the distance around), area measures the space covered inside the shape.

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Negative Numbers on a Number Line
tasks.content: A number line extends in both directions from zero: positive numbers to the right, negative numbers to the left. Negative numbers represent values below zero, like temperatures below freezing (-5 degrees) or a lift going below ground level (-2). The further left a number is on the number line, the smaller its value, even though it might look 'bigger' without the minus sign.

levels.levelName: Adding & Subtracting Fractions with the Same Denominator

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Adding & Subtracting Fractions with the Same Denominator
tasks.content: When fractions have the same denominator (bottom number), you can add or subtract them by just adding or subtracting the numerators (top numbers) and keeping the denominator the same. For example, 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5, and 4/7 - 2/7 = 2/7. The denominator stays the same because it tells you the size of each part, which doesn't change.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A shape has line symmetry if it can be folded along a line so both halves match up exactly - that fold line is called the line of symmetry. A square has 4 lines of symmetry, while a rectangle (that isn't a square) has only 2. Some shapes, like a scalene triangle, have no lines of symmetry at all because no fold makes both sides match.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Translating a shape means sliding it to a new position without rotating, flipping, or resizing it - every point moves the same distance in the same direction. A translation can be described as moving a certain number of units left/right and up/down, like 'translate 3 right and 2 up'.

tasks.content: Tamil verbs change their ending to show kaalam (காலம், tense): past, present, and future. Using the verb செல் (go): நிகழ்காலம் (present) gives செல்கிறேன் (I go/am going); இறந்தகாலம் (past) gives சென்றேன் (I went); எதிர்காலம் (future) gives செல்வேன் (I will go). Practice conjugating படி (study/read) into all three tenses: படிக்கிறேன் (I study), படித்தேன் (I studied), படிப்பேன் (I will study).

tasks.content: Synonyms, ottha sollugal (ஒத்த சொற்கள்), are words with similar meanings, like மகிழ்ச்சி and சந்தோஷம் (both mean happiness). tasks.content: A pazhamozhi (பழமொழி) is a traditional Tamil proverb passed down through generations, often teaching wisdom in a few words. tasks.content: A compound word, thodarsol (தொடர்ச்சொல்), is formed by joining two words together to make a new meaning. பள்ளி (school) + கூடம் (hall) becomes பள்ளிக்கூடம் (schoolhouse/school). மாம் (mango tree) + பழம் (fruit) becomes மாம்பழம் (mango). tasks.content: Different animal groups have very different life cycles: a mammal, like a human or a dog, is born live and grows through stages to adulthood, while an amphibian, like a frog, begins as an egg, hatches into a swimming tadpole, and metamorphoses into an adult that can live on land. An insect, like a butterfly, goes through complete metamorphosis, changing from egg to larva to pupa to adult, and a bird, like a robin, hatches from an egg and is fed by its parents until it can fly. Living things also reproduce in different ways: many animals reproduce sexually, where a male and female parent are needed, while some plants can also reproduce using seeds formed after pollination, or grow new plants from runners or bulbs.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Humans go through several distinct stages as they grow older, from birth through to old age. After birth, a baby grows through infancy and early childhood, developing quickly in size and ability, before becoming a child and then reaching adolescence, or puberty, when the body changes rapidly to become an adult body. Adulthood is the longest stage of the human life cycle, during which the body is fully grown, before people eventually reach old age, when the body gradually becomes less able to do the things it once could.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Materials can be compared and grouped by their properties, including hardness, whether they let electricity or heat pass through, whether they dissolve in water, and whether they are magnetic. A material that dissolves in water, like sugar or salt, forms a solution, while a material like sand does not dissolve and remains as separate particles mixed with the water. Different mixtures can be separated using methods that match their properties, such as using a sieve to separate large stones from smaller sand, filtering to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid, or evaporating a solution to leave the dissolved solid behind.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Our solar system is made up of the sun at its centre, with eight planets, including Earth, travelling around it in paths called orbits. Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are the four rocky planets closest to the sun, while Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are much larger gas giants further out. Earth takes approximately 365 days, or one year, to complete a single orbit around the sun, and the moon, in turn, orbits around the Earth roughly every 27 to 28 days.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Gravity is a force that pulls objects towards the Earth, which is why a dropped ball falls to the ground instead of floating away. When objects move through air or water, they experience resistance forces that act against their motion: air resistance slows down things like a falling parachute or a moving bicycle, while water resistance, sometimes called drag, slows down a swimmer or a boat moving through water. A streamlined shape, like that of a dolphin or a racing car, reduces resistance and lets the object move more easily through air or water.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Simple mechanisms help us use a smaller force to achieve a bigger effect, making everyday tasks easier. A lever, like a seesaw or a pair of scissors, is a rigid bar that pivots around a fixed point called a fulcrum, allowing a small push to lift a heavier load. A pulley uses a wheel and rope to change the direction of a force, making it easier to lift heavy objects, such as raising a flag up a flagpole, while gears are toothed wheels that lock together so that turning one gear turns another, changing the speed or direction of movement, as seen in a bicycle's gears.

tasks.content: Some changes to materials are reversible, meaning the material can be changed back to how it was before, such as melting ice, which can be frozen again, or dissolving salt in water, which can be recovered by evaporating the water. Other changes are irreversible, meaning a new material is formed and the change cannot be undone, such as burning wood to make ash and smoke, baking a cake from raw ingredients, or an iron nail rusting when it reacts with oxygen and water. Mixing vinegar with bicarbonate of soda is a good classroom example of an irreversible change, because it creates new substances and produces bubbles of gas.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Day and night happen because the Earth spins, or rotates, on its own axis once approximately every 24 hours, meaning different parts of the Earth face towards or away from the sun at different times. When your part of the Earth faces the sun, it is daytime, and when it has rotated to face away from the sun, it is night. The seasons occur because the Earth is slightly tilted on its axis as it orbits the sun over the year, meaning different parts of the Earth receive more or less direct sunlight at different times, making summer warmer with longer days and winter colder with shorter days.

tasks.content: After collecting results from an investigation, a scientist needs to evaluate the evidence, which means looking carefully at what the data shows and deciding how reliable and trustworthy it is. This involves checking whether the results support the original prediction, spotting any results that look unusual or anomalous compared to the rest, and thinking about whether the test was carried out fairly. Evaluating evidence also means considering whether repeating the test, or using more measurements, would make the conclusion more certain and trustworthy.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Electricity flows through a complete circuit - a loop of wire connecting a power source (like a battery) to a component (like a bulb), with no gaps. If the circuit is broken (an open circuit), electricity can't flow and the bulb won't light. Materials that let electricity flow through them easily are called conductors (like metal), while materials that block it are called insulators (like plastic or rubber).

tasks.content: Sound is created by vibrations - when an object vibrates (moves back and forth quickly), it makes the air around it vibrate too, creating sound waves that travel to our ears. tasks.taskName: Lesson: Repetition and Loops: Going Deeper
tasks.content: We already know that a loop repeats a group of instructions, but this year we look more closely at different types of loops and how to choose the right one for a task. A count-controlled loop, such as repeat 10 times, runs a set number of times that we decide in advance, and is useful when we already know exactly how many repetitions we need, such as drawing a shape with a known number of sides. A condition-controlled loop, sometimes called a repeat until loop, keeps repeating until a certain condition becomes true, which is useful when we do not know in advance exactly how many times the loop needs to run. For example, repeat until the player reaches the finish line will keep looping for as long as needed, whether that takes five steps or fifty. It is also possible to nest loops, which means putting one loop inside another loop, useful for tasks like drawing a grid of squares, where an outer loop controls the rows and an inner loop controls the columns within each row. Choosing the right type of loop makes a program more efficient and easier to understand, and helps avoid problems such as infinite loops, where a loop never stops because its condition can never become true, which can cause a program to freeze.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Variables and selection become much more powerful when they are used together, because a program can check the value stored in a variable and then decide what to do based on that value. For example, imagine a program with a variable called lives, which starts at 3. Every time the player is hit, the program might subtract 1 from lives, and then use a selection block to check if lives is equal to 0. If this condition is true, the program can display game over, but if it is false, the game simply carries on as normal. This combination of variables and selection lets programs make sensible decisions that change depending on what has happened while the program is running, rather than always doing exactly the same thing. We can also use comparison operators to build conditions, such as checking if a variable is equal to, greater than, or less than a certain number, for example if score is greater than or equal to 100, then say you reached the high score. Combining variables and selection is one of the most useful skills in programming, because it allows programs, especially games, to respond intelligently to changing information, such as scores, lives, time remaining, or a player's choices.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A flowchart is a diagram that shows the steps of an algorithm using different shapes connected by arrows, making it easier to plan and understand a program before writing any code. Each shape in a flowchart has a specific meaning. An oval shape usually shows the start or end of the algorithm. A rectangle shows a step or an instruction to be carried out, such as add 1 to score. A diamond shape shows a decision, which is a question with a yes or no, or true or false, answer, matching the idea of selection that we have already learned. Arrows connect the shapes and show the order in which the steps should happen, and when a diamond decision is used, two arrows usually lead out of it, one for each possible answer, showing the different paths the algorithm could take. Flowcharts are especially useful for planning algorithms that include selection or loops, because they let us see the different possible paths through the algorithm clearly, before we try to build it using code. For example, a flowchart for checking if a password is correct might show a decision diamond asking is the password correct, with one path leading to allow access, and another path leading back to try again. Drawing a flowchart before coding helps us spot missing steps or confusing logic early on.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Debugging Strategies: Finding Logic Errors
tasks.content: As programs become more complex, using variables, selection, and loops together, bugs can become trickier to find, especially a type of bug called a logic error. A logic error happens when a program runs without crashing or showing an obvious error message, but it still produces the wrong result, because the instructions do not do quite what we intended. Logic errors can be some of the hardest bugs to find, precisely because the program appears to be working. One useful debugging strategy is called tracing, where we go through the program step by step, exactly as the computer would, writing down the value of each variable as it changes, to see exactly where the result starts to go wrong. Another useful strategy is to test the program with different inputs, including unusual or extreme ones, because a bug might only appear in certain situations, such as when a variable reaches exactly zero. It also helps to check conditions very carefully, because a small mistake, such as using greater than instead of greater than or equal to, can completely change how a selection block behaves. Reading code aloud, or explaining it to someone else line by line, often helps us notice mistakes that we have been reading past without seeing. Careful, patient, methodical debugging is what separates confusing, broken programs from clear, reliable ones.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Simulating Physical Systems with Code
tasks.content: Programs can be used to simulate, or imitate, how things behave in the real world, which is a powerful use of computing in science, engineering, and games. A simulation uses code, including variables, selection, and loops, to model a real system and show how it might change over time. For example, we could simulate a bouncing ball using a variable for its height, and a loop that repeatedly reduces the height slightly to show it falling, then uses selection to check if the ball has reached the ground, and if so, makes it bounce back upward instead of continuing to fall. Another example is simulating a simple traffic light system, using a sequence and a loop to make a light cycle through red, then red and amber together, then green, then amber, before repeating the whole sequence again, matching how real traffic lights behave. Simulations are useful because they let us explore how a system works, test out different situations safely, and predict what might happen, without needing the real physical object, which can sometimes be expensive, dangerous, or simply impossible to test directly, such as simulating weather patterns or the orbit of planets. Building a simple simulation combines everything we have learned about sequence, selection, loops, and variables into one program that models something real.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Data and Information: Collecting and Presenting
tasks.content: Data means raw facts and figures, such as numbers or short pieces of text, which by themselves may not tell us very much. Information is what we get once data has been organised, processed, or explained in a way that makes it meaningful and useful. For example, a single number like 24 is just data, but if we say the temperature today is 24 degrees Celsius, that number has become useful information. In computing, we often collect data using tools such as questionnaires, tally charts, or sensors that automatically measure things like temperature or light levels. Once data has been collected, it usually needs to be organised, for example by entering it into a spreadsheet, sorting it into categories, or counting how often something appears. After data has been organised, we can present it clearly using tables, charts, or graphs, which often make patterns and comparisons much easier to see than looking at a long list of raw numbers. For example, a bar chart can quickly show which class had the most pupils walk to school, something that might be hard to notice by reading a plain list. Choosing the right way to present data, and making sure charts have clear titles and labels, helps other people understand our information quickly and accurately.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A database is an organised collection of information, stored on a computer, so that it can be easily searched, sorted, and updated. Databases are usually organised into tables, which look similar to a spreadsheet, made up of rows and columns. Each row in a table is called a record, and represents one complete set of information about a single thing, such as one pupil, one book, or one product. Each column is called a field, and represents one particular piece of information collected about every record, such as name, age, or favourite colour. For example, a simple school library database might have a table where each record is one book, and the fields include title, author, and whether the book is currently available to borrow. One of the most useful things about a database is that we can search it, using specific criteria, to quickly find matching records, for example searching for every book written by a particular author, without needing to look through a long list by hand. We can also sort a database, for example putting all the books in order by title or by author's surname, and we can filter it, showing only the records that match certain conditions, such as only books that are currently available. Databases are used constantly in real life, including school registers, library systems, medical records, and online shops.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: How Search Engines Rank Results
tasks.content: When we search for something online, a search engine does not simply show us every website that mentions our search words in a random order. Instead, it uses a set of rules and calculations, called an algorithm, to work out which results are most likely to be useful, and shows the results ranked with the most relevant ones near the top of the list. Search engines look at many different clues to decide how to rank a webpage. One important clue is relevance, which means how closely the words and content on a page match what we searched for. Another important clue is how trustworthy or popular a website seems to be, which search engines can partly judge by how many other reliable websites link to it, a bit like how a well-recommended shop might be trusted more than one nobody has ever mentioned. Search engines also consider how well a website works, such as whether it loads quickly and works properly on a phone or tablet, not just a computer. Because search engines use algorithms to rank results, and because some website owners try hard to appear near the top of search results, it is still important to think carefully about the results we click on, and remember that being ranked first does not automatically mean a website is completely accurate or trustworthy, only that a search engine's algorithm judged it as likely to be relevant and useful.
Let's practice what we just learned!
