tasks.taskName: Lesson: Online Safety: Cyberbullying and Reporting
tasks.content: Cyberbullying means using technology, such as messaging apps, games, or social media, to deliberately upset, embarrass, threaten, or be unkind to someone, repeatedly and on purpose. It can include sending unkind or threatening messages, spreading untrue or hurtful rumours online, deliberately leaving someone out of online groups or games, or sharing embarrassing pictures or videos of someone without their permission. Cyberbullying can feel especially difficult because it can follow a person outside of school, sometimes even into their own home, and hurtful messages can be seen again and again, or shared further to other people. It is important to remember that cyberbullying is never the fault of the person experiencing it, and nobody deserves to be treated that way. If cyberbullying happens to you, or you see it happening to somebody else, the most important step is to tell a trusted adult, such as a parent, carer, or teacher, straight away, rather than dealing with it alone or in secret. Most apps, games, and websites also have a reporting or blocking feature, which allows us to report unkind behaviour to the people who run the website, and to block a person so they can no longer contact us. Keeping evidence, such as not deleting a hurtful message straight away, can also help a trusted adult understand exactly what happened and how to help.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Creating a multimedia presentation means combining several types of media, such as text, images, sound, and sometimes video, into a single organised project that explains an idea clearly to an audience. Before creating slides, it helps to plan the whole presentation first, deciding on the overall purpose, the main points to be covered, and a sensible order for those points, so that the presentation flows logically from beginning to end. Each slide should usually focus on just one main idea, with a short, clear heading, and only as much text as is needed, because slides that are too crowded with writing can be hard for an audience to read and follow. Images should be chosen carefully to support and illustrate the point being made on that slide, rather than being added just to fill space, and any sound or narration should be clear and add real value, rather than distracting from the message. It is also important to check that the presentation is consistent, using similar fonts, colours, and layouts throughout, so it looks professional and organised rather than messy. Once the presentation is finished, it is worth practising going through it, checking that everything works correctly, that the information is accurate, and that the order of slides makes logical sense, before sharing it with an audience.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Every sprite in Scratch can have more than one costume, which are different pictures or poses that make up how the sprite looks. Think of costumes like frames in a flip book: each one is slightly different, and when you flip through them quickly, one after another, it creates the illusion of movement, even though each costume is really just a still picture. This is exactly how sprite animation works in Scratch! For example, a walking cat sprite might have two costumes, one with its legs together, and one with its legs apart, mid-step. If we switch back and forth between these two costumes quickly, using the "next costume" block inside a loop, combined with a small "wait" block between each switch, the cat will appear to actually be walking, even though we are just swapping between two simple pictures over and over. The "next costume" block automatically moves to the very next costume in the sprite's costume list, and after the last costume, it loops back around to the first one again. We can also switch directly to a specific costume by name, using the "switch costume to" block, which is useful for showing an exact pose at an exact moment, like switching to a "surprised" costume the instant a sprite touches something unexpected. Good animation usually combines costume changes with motion blocks at the same time, so a character is not just changing its look, but also actually traveling across the stage, just like the walking cat example. The timing of the "wait" block matters quite a lot too: too short a wait and the animation looks like a blur, too long a wait and it looks jerky and slow instead of smooth. Today we will look at a sprite's costume list, build a walking or flying animation using "next costume" inside a loop, and adjust our wait times until the motion looks smooth and natural.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: So far, each sprite's code has mostly worked on its own, but what if we want one sprite's actions to affect a completely different sprite? That is exactly what broadcasting is for! Broadcasting lets one sprite send a message that any other sprite in the project can listen for and react to, even though the sprites are not directly connected to each other in any other way. To use broadcasting, we use two special event blocks: "broadcast message," which sends out a chosen message to the entire project, and "when I receive message," which starts a script on any sprite that is listening for that exact same message. For example, imagine a game where a wizard sprite casts a spell, and we want a dragon sprite, somewhere else in the project, to disappear the moment the spell is cast. We could give the wizard sprite a script that broadcasts a message called "spell cast" the moment the spell button is pressed. Then, on the dragon sprite, we would build a separate script that starts with "when I receive spell cast," followed by a "hide" block, making the dragon disappear at exactly the right moment. Notice that the wizard sprite does not need to know anything at all about the dragon sprite, it just broadcasts the message out into the whole project, and any sprite that cares can react however it wants to. This makes broadcasting incredibly powerful for coordinating many sprites at once, like starting a whole scene change, or signaling that a level is complete, without needing to write complicated code connecting every single sprite directly to every other sprite. Today we will build a two-sprite project where one sprite broadcasts a message and a second sprite reacts to it, testing what happens when the message is sent at different times.

tasks.content: In Grade 2, we had a first, simple look at loops within loops. Now, as our Scratch projects grow more advanced, let's dive deeper into nested loops, loops placed inside other loops, and see how powerful they can be for creating patterns and repeated behaviors. When we nest a loop inside another loop, the inner loop must completely finish all of its repeats before the outer loop can continue on to its next repeat. Let's look at a drawing example using the pen blocks in Scratch: imagine we want to draw a grid of dots, three rows of dots, with five dots in each row. We could use an outer loop that says "repeat 3," for the three rows, and inside it, an inner loop that says "repeat 5," for the five dots in each row, with a "stamp" block and a "move" block inside the inner loop to actually draw each dot and move over slightly before drawing the next one. After the inner loop finishes drawing all five dots in a row, the outer loop would move the pen down to the next row, and then the inner loop would run again, drawing five more dots. In total, this nested loop would draw fifteen dots, three rows multiplied by five dots each. Nested loops are also extremely useful for animations, like a sprite that needs to blink twice, every time it takes a step, for several steps in a row, in which case the blinking would be the inner loop, and the stepping would be the outer loop. When working with nested loops, it helps to think about which action is the "big" repeating action, which becomes the outer loop, and which action is the "small" repeating action that happens inside each big repeat, which becomes the inner loop. Today we will use nested loops with pen blocks to draw a simple repeated shape pattern, calculating ahead of time exactly how many total shapes our nested loops should create.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In Grade 3, we learned about the if-then block, which runs certain blocks only when a condition is true, and skips them otherwise. This year, we are learning about its more powerful cousin: the if-else block! An if-else block still checks whether a condition is true or false, but now it has two separate sets of blocks: one set that runs if the condition is true, and a completely different set that runs if the condition is false, instead of simply being skipped. This means an if-else block always runs something, either the "if" part or the "else" part, never both, and never neither. Let's think of an example: a quiz game sprite that checks whether a player clicked the correct answer. Using if-else, we could write: "if answer is correct, then say Great job! and change score by 1, else say Try again! and change lives by negative 1." Notice how both outcomes, getting it right and getting it wrong, are handled within a single block, instead of needing two completely separate if-then blocks checking opposite conditions. This makes our code shorter, clearer, and much less likely to have mistakes, since we do not have to remember to write a second, opposite condition ourselves. If-else blocks are perfect anytime there are exactly two possible outcomes: win or lose, open or closed, day or night, touching or not touching. When there might be three or more possible outcomes, coders often use several if-else blocks together, or a similar block called "if-else if," which we may explore in later grades. Today we will convert a project that uses two separate if-then blocks into a single, cleaner if-else block, and we will build a new script from scratch using if-else to handle a true and false outcome differently.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Operators: Math and Comparison Blocks
tasks.content: Operator blocks in Scratch are green, and they let our programs do math and make comparisons, which is especially useful when combined with variables and if-else blocks. Math operator blocks include addition, like "__ + __", subtraction, like "__ - __", multiplication, and division, letting our programs calculate numbers while the project is running, instead of us calculating everything by hand ahead of time. Comparison operator blocks, on the other hand, compare two values and return either true or false, which makes them perfect for fitting inside the hexagon-shaped condition slot of an if-then or if-else block. The three main comparison operators are greater than, shown as "__ > __", less than, shown as "__ < __", and equal to, shown as "__ = __". For example, imagine a game where a player wins once their score reaches 10 points. We could use an if-then block with the condition "score > 9", or equally correctly, "score = 10", to check whether the player has reached the winning score, and then show a "You win!" message once that condition becomes true. Operators can also be combined with each other, like using multiplication inside an addition block, letting us build more complex math expressions out of simple building blocks, the same way we snap together motion or sound blocks. There are also operators for combining true and false conditions, like "and", "or", and "not", which let us check multiple conditions at the same time, such as "if score > 9 and lives > 0", which would only be true if both parts are true at the very same time. Today we will practice building simple math expressions with operator blocks, and we will use comparison operators inside if-then and if-else blocks to check score and lives conditions in a sample project.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Using Variables for Score and Lives

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Using Variables for Score and Lives
tasks.content: We first learned about variables in Grade 3, using them to keep score. This year, we will go further, using multiple variables together, like score and lives, to build more complete and realistic games. Just like score, a lives variable stores a number, usually starting at a value like 3, representing how many chances a player has before the game ends. As the game runs, we use "change lives by -1" whenever the player makes a mistake, like a sprite getting hit by an obstacle, and we use an if-then block to check whether lives has reached 0, which would trigger the game to end. Combining score and lives together creates much more interesting games than using either variable alone. For example, imagine a game where a player collects coins to increase their score, but loses a life every time they touch a spike. We would need an if-then block checking "touching coin" that leads to "change score by 1", and a separate if-then block checking "touching spike" that leads to "change lives by -1", and then another if-then block checking "lives = 0" that leads to broadcasting a "game over" message. Because variables can be shown on the stage, players can watch both their score and their remaining lives update in real time as they play, which makes the game feel exciting and keeps players motivated to keep trying. It is also important to reset variables back to their starting values, like setting score to 0 and lives to 3, using "set" blocks connected to the green flag event, so that every new game starts fresh instead of continuing from the numbers left over by the last time the game was played. Today we will build a small game using both a score variable and a lives variable together, making sure both reset correctly at the start of a new game.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A variable can only hold one piece of information at a time, like a single score number. But what if we need to remember many pieces of information at once, like a list of high scores, or the names of several players? That is exactly what a list is for! A list is like a variable, but instead of one box, it is a whole row of numbered boxes, each one able to hold its own separate piece of information. In Scratch, lists appear alongside variables, shown as an orange block category, and they can be shown on the stage just like variables can, displaying every item in the list at once. To use a list, we first create it and give it a name, like "high scores." Then we can use blocks like "add __ to list," which adds a new item to the very end of the list, "delete __ of list," which removes an item at a specific position, and "item __ of list," which lets us look up and use whatever is stored at a specific position in the list. For example, imagine a game that keeps track of the five most recent scores from different rounds played. Every time a round ends, we could use "add score to high scores," adding the newest score to the end of the list, building up a growing record over time. We could also use a loop combined with "item __ of list" to display every single score stored in the list, one at a time, perhaps showing them as a scrolling record of past attempts. Lists are incredibly useful anytime a program needs to keep track of more than one piece of information, like a shopping list, a set of player names, or a collection of words for a spelling game. Today we will create a list, add several items to it using blocks, and use a loop to display every item stored inside it.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: As our projects use more and more variables, like score, lives, and lists, a new and very useful debugging skill becomes important: using variables themselves to help us find bugs! One of the best debugging tricks in Scratch is to show a variable on the stage while testing a project, watching its value change in real time as the project runs, instead of guessing whether it is working correctly. For example, if a score variable is not increasing the way we expect when a sprite touches a coin, we can show the score variable on the stage and watch closely: does it increase at all? Does it increase by the wrong amount, like 2 instead of 1? Does it increase at the wrong time, like when touching the wrong sprite instead of the coin? Watching the variable update, or fail to update, gives us important clues about exactly where the mistake might be hiding. Another useful trick is creating a temporary "debug" variable specifically to track information while we are testing, even if we plan to remove it later, once everything works correctly. For example, we might create a variable called "debug" and set it to show which if-then block condition most recently became true, helping us understand the order that different parts of our code are actually running in, which is not always obvious just by reading the blocks. We can also use lists for debugging, adding a short message to a list every time an important event happens in our code, building up a kind of history log we can look back through afterward to see exactly what happened, and in what order. Today we will intentionally break a working project by changing one variable-related block, and we will use variable-watching techniques to find and fix the mistake.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Building a Maze or Chase Game

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Building a Maze or Chase Game
tasks.content: Now let's combine everything we have learned this year, costumes and animation, broadcasting, nested loops, if-else blocks, operators, variables for score and lives, and lists, into one exciting final type of project: a maze or chase game! In a maze game, a sprite must navigate through a path filled with walls, using arrow key events and motion blocks, while an if-then block continuously checks whether the sprite is touching a wall color, sending it back to the start if it bumps into one. In a chase game, instead of walls, one sprite, like a player-controlled character, is chased by another sprite, controlled by code instead of a player, using motion blocks combined with a loop that constantly points and moves the chaser toward the player's position. Building a full maze or chase game requires planning: first, sketch the maze layout or the chase area on paper. Second, decide exactly how the player will control their sprite, usually with arrow key events. Third, decide what makes the player win, like reaching a goal spot in a maze, and what makes the player lose, like running out of lives after being caught by a chaser. Fourth, decide where variables are needed, like a lives variable that decreases each time the chaser catches the player, or a timer that counts down. As we build, we will use if-else blocks to handle two-way outcomes, like whether the player reached the goal or not, operators to compare positions or scores, and broadcasting to signal important moments, like starting a new level or ending the game. This project brings together nearly every single coding concept we have learned since Grade 1, from simple sequencing all the way up to lists and operators. Today we will begin planning and building our own maze or chase game, working through each planning question before opening Scratch to start building.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: You have reached the end of an amazing year of coding, and your skills have grown enormously! This year, you learned to animate sprites using costumes, send broadcast messages between sprites, build nested loops for complex repeating patterns, make two-way decisions with if-else blocks, use operator blocks for math and comparisons, track score and lives with variables, store multiple pieces of information using lists, debug using variables and history logs, and even design a full maze or chase game. For your final mini project of the year, you will design and build a complete Scratch project that shows off as many of these skills as possible, working almost entirely on your own, just like a real programmer. Begin, as always, with planning: What is your project about? What sprites, costumes, and backgrounds will you need? What events will control the action? Where will you need loops, if-then or if-else blocks, variables, or even a list? Sketch your plan on paper before opening Scratch, listing out the blocks and concepts you expect to use. As you build, work in small, testable pieces, just like we have practiced all year, checking that each part works correctly before adding the next one. Use your debugging skills whenever something does not behave the way you expect, watching your variables, checking your event blocks, and looking closely at your if-then and if-else conditions. When your project is complete, take time to test it thoroughly, trying to "break" it on purpose by doing unexpected things, like clicking sprites in a strange order, to make sure it still behaves correctly. Finally, share your finished project with classmates, and take time to explore theirs as well, noticing the different, creative ways everyone combined the very same coding tools. You have built a strong foundation in coding this year, and you are ready to take on even bigger and more exciting challenges in the future. Great work, coder!
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A platformer game has a character that runs and jumps across platforms, avoiding obstacles or enemies to reach a goal. tasks.content: Summarising means capturing a text's key points in far fewer words than the original, using your own phrasing rather than copying sentences. A strong summary keeps the main ideas and cuts repetition, examples and minor detail. Critical analysis goes further: it asks whether the writer's argument is convincing, what evidence they use, and whether their viewpoint might be biased or one-sided. Skilled readers separate what a text says (fact) from what it wants you to think (opinion).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In the active voice, the subject of the sentence performs the action, as in 'The dog chased the ball.' In the passive voice, the subject receives the action instead, as in 'The ball was chased by the dog,' formed with a form of 'to be' plus a past participle. Writers choose the passive voice to focus attention on the action or the receiver rather than who did it, or when the doer is unknown or unimportant, as in 'The window was broken.' Recognising both forms helps you control emphasis and formality in your own writing.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The subjunctive mood is used for hypothetical, wished-for or formal situations, such as 'If I were you, I would apologise' or 'The teacher insisted that he arrive on time.' Notice that the verb form often differs from ordinary agreement, for example using 'were' instead of 'was' for all subjects, or the base form of the verb after words like 'suggest,' 'demand' or 'insist.' The subjunctive is common in formal or written English and signals that something is imagined, wished for, or required rather than a plain fact.

tasks.content: Cohesion is what makes a piece of writing flow as one connected whole rather than a list of separate sentences. Writers achieve this using adverbials (such as 'meanwhile,' 'as a result,' 'later that day') to link ideas across paragraphs, pronouns to avoid repeating nouns, and deliberate repetition or synonyms to keep a reader tracking the same idea. Strong cohesion guides the reader smoothly from one point to the next without confusing jumps.

tasks.content: A colon introduces a list, an explanation or an example, as in 'She packed three things: a map, a torch and water.' A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction, as in 'The rain stopped; the sun came out,' or separates items in a complex list. A hyphen joins words to form a compound, such as 'well-known' or 'long-term,' and can prevent ambiguity, as in 're-cover' versus 'recover.' Choosing the right mark makes your meaning precise.

tasks.content: Extended narrative writing means planning and sustaining a story across multiple paragraphs or chapters rather than a single short scene. Strong long-form stories need a clear structure — an opening that establishes character and setting, rising action with complications, a climax, and a resolution — plus consistent characters and a controlled pace. Planning a story arc before you write helps you avoid rushing the ending or losing track of subplots, and revisiting earlier details, like a promise or an object, later in the story builds satisfying cohesion.

tasks.content: Journalistic writing reports events in a clear, factual style while sometimes including opinion in clearly labelled sections such as comment or editorial pieces. News reports typically open with a headline and a strong first paragraph answering who, what, when, where and why, then add supporting facts, quotations and details in order of importance — a structure called the 'inverted pyramid.' Good journalism keeps fact and opinion clearly separate, uses quotations to add authority, and writes in a tone suited to its audience.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Poets choose form (the shape and structure of a poem, such as its stanza pattern, line length or rhyme scheme) and imagery (descriptive language that appeals to the senses, including metaphor and simile) to create effect and meaning beyond the literal words. A short, fragmented line might mirror a character's breathlessness or shock, while a regular rhythm can suggest calm or inevitability. When analysing a poem, ask not just what an image means but why the poet placed it exactly where they did, and what that structural choice adds to the poem's meaning.
Let's practice what we just learned!

options: the poem's structure, such as stanza pattern, line length and rhyme

tasks.content: Effective spoken argument requires a clear structure: state your point, support it with evidence or reasoning, and address opposing views before summarising. Good debaters adapt their tone, pace and vocabulary to their audience, use rhetorical techniques such as rhetorical questions and the rule of three to persuade, and listen actively so they can respond to counter-arguments rather than simply repeating prepared points. Preparing key points in advance, along with anticipated objections, builds confidence for formal spoken argument.
Let's practice what we just learned!

options: move immediately to a new topic

because it is required by law

questions.questionText: Which closing technique most effectively ends a spoken argument?

tasks.content: In debate and argument writing, you present a clear point of view (your argument), back it up with reasons and evidence, and often acknowledge the other side's point of view before explaining why your argument is still stronger (a counter-argument). Structuring an argument with a clear introduction, points in order of importance, and a strong conclusion makes it far more convincing.

It removes the need for evidence

Setting is where and when a story happens, and can affect mood (a dark forest feels tense, a sunny beach feels relaxed). When analysing a text, look closely at word choices to understand what the writer wants you to feel about a character or place.

tasks.content: A newspaper report answers the key questions: who, what, when, where, why and how. It starts with a catchy headline, then an opening paragraph that summarises the main facts, followed by more detail in order of importance (most important first). Reports are usually written in third person and past tense, using facts and sometimes quotes from people involved, rather than personal opinion.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.correctAnswer: Who, what, when, where, why, how

tasks.content: A fronted adverbial is a word or phrase placed at the start of a sentence to describe when, where or how something happens, followed by a comma - like 'Suddenly, the door opened' or 'After the storm, we went outside.' Starting a sentence this way adds variety and emphasises the time, place or manner before the main action.

tasks.content: A relative clause adds extra information about a noun, usually starting with 'who', 'which', 'that' or 'whose' - like 'The dog, which was very old, slept all day.' tasks.content: Balanced argument writing presents both sides of an issue fairly, using phrases like 'on the other hand' or 'however' to move between viewpoints, before reaching a reasoned conclusion. tasks.content: A story told in first person uses 'I' and 'we', as if the narrator is a character inside the story, like 'I ran through the forest, my heart pounding'. tasks.content: Cohesive devices are words and phrases that link ideas together across sentences and paragraphs, making writing flow smoothly instead of feeling disconnected. Examples include 'furthermore' (to add a point), 'therefore' (to show a result), and 'meanwhile' (to show something happening at the same time).

questions.questionText: What happens to writing without good cohesive devices?

tasks.content: A flashback interrupts the main story to show an earlier event, often to explain a character's feelings or give background information the reader needs. tasks.content: Every digit in a large number has a value based on its column: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, millions, and ten millions. In 6,428,571 the 6 is worth 6,000,000, the 4 is worth 400,000, and so on, so we can partition it as 6,000,000 + 400,000 + 20,000 + 8,000 + 500 + 70 + 1. To round a number, look at the digit to the right of the column you are rounding to: 6,482,913 rounded to the nearest 100,000 is 6,500,000, because the ten-thousands digit (8) rounds up.

For addition and subtraction, line up the columns and carry or borrow as needed: 3,847 + 2,956 = 6,803. For short division, divide each digit in turn and carry remainders: 4,236 divided by 6 is 706, because 6 x 706 = 4,236. To change a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator; to change a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100. For example, 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. To simplify a decimal into a fraction, write it over 100 (or 1000) and cancel down: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

For example, to share £24 in the ratio 3:5, there are 8 parts in total, so each part is £3, giving shares of £9 and £15.

Imperial units are still used in everyday life alongside them, and rough conversions are useful: 1 mile is approximately 1.6km, and 1kg is approximately 2.2 pounds. tasks.content: A compound shape is made of two or more basic shapes joined together, so to find its area, split it into rectangles or triangles, find each area separately, then add (or subtract, if a piece has been removed) them. Perimeter is the total distance around the outside, found by adding every outer side length. For example, an L-shape made from a 6cm by 4cm rectangle and a 3cm by 2cm rectangle has a total area of 24 + 6 = 30cm².

tasks.content: The mean (average) of a set of numbers is found by adding them all together, then dividing by how many numbers there are. For the numbers 4, 6, 8, the mean is (4+6+8) / 3 = 18 / 3 = 6. The mean gives a single number that represents the 'typical' value of a data set.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A formula is a rule written using letters (variables) that shows how to calculate something, like the perimeter of a square: P = 4s (where s is the side length). Substitution means replacing the letters with actual numbers to calculate a result - if s = 5, then P = 4 x 5 = 20.

tasks.content: Living things are sorted into groups based on shared characteristics, a process called classification. Scientists use a hierarchy including kingdoms such as animals, plants, fungi and microorganisms, and within animals further groups like vertebrates and invertebrates. Classification keys, such as branching (dichotomous) keys, ask yes/no questions to help identify an unknown organism. Grouping living things this way helps scientists communicate clearly and spot patterns in how organisms are related.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Inheritance is the passing of characteristics from parents to offspring through genetic information. Offspring resemble their parents but are not identical to them or to each other, because of variation. Evolution is the gradual change in species over many generations, driven by natural selection: organisms with characteristics best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those characteristics on. Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection explains how today's wide variety of species developed from earlier life forms over millions of years.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The circulatory system moves blood around the body, carrying oxygen and nutrients to cells and removing waste products like carbon dioxide. The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers that pushes blood through a network of blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry blood back to the heart, and tiny capillaries connect them and allow exchange of substances with body tissues. Blood itself contains red blood cells, which carry oxygen using a substance called haemoglobin, as well as white blood cells that fight infection and plasma that carries dissolved substances.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A healthy, balanced diet provides the right nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water) in the correct amounts for the body's needs, which vary with age, activity level and health. Regular exercise keeps the heart and muscles strong and helps maintain a healthy body weight, while too little exercise or an unbalanced diet can lead to health problems such as obesity or malnutrition. Drugs, including legal ones like alcohol, tobacco and caffeine, change how the body functions and can harm health, particularly the heart, lungs and liver, which is why understanding their effects on lifestyle is important.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: We see objects because light travels from a light source, bounces (reflects) off objects, and enters our eyes. Light enters through the transparent cornea and pupil, and the lens focuses it onto the retina at the back of the eye, where light-sensitive cells detect it. The retina converts the light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to the brain, where the image is interpreted. Light travels in straight lines, which is why we can only see an object if there is a straight, unblocked path from it to our eyes.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols to show how components are connected in an electrical circuit, making it easy for anyone to read and build the same circuit. Common symbols include a straight line for a wire, a circle with a line through it for a cell (battery), a circle with a cross for a bulb, a zigzag or rectangle for a resistor, and a break in a line with a lever for a switch. In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop one after another, so if one component is removed or breaks, the whole circuit stops working.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Adaptations are special features or behaviours that help a living thing survive and reproduce in its particular habitat. Structural adaptations are physical features, such as a polar bear's thick fur and fat for warmth in the Arctic, or a cactus's spines and thick stem for storing water in the desert. Behavioural adaptations are things an animal does, such as migrating to warmer places or hibernating through winter to save energy. Over many generations, species become well suited to their environment through natural selection, but if their habitat changes too quickly they may struggle to survive.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A full scientific investigation starts with a clear question and a prediction of what you expect to happen and why. You then plan a fair test by identifying the independent variable (the one thing you change), the dependent variable (what you measure), and the control variables (everything kept the same), along with choosing suitable equipment and repeating measurements for reliability. After carrying out the investigation safely, results are recorded in a table, often displayed in a graph, and then used to draw a conclusion that answers the original question, explaining whether the prediction was correct.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Science reasoning questions test how well you can apply scientific knowledge to new situations, interpret data from tables and graphs, and explain your thinking using evidence. This often involves reading a short passage or looking at results, then answering questions that ask you to identify patterns, make comparisons, or explain why something happened using the correct scientific vocabulary. Practising these skills, similar to those used in KS2 SATs, helps you show not just what you know, but how well you can think and reason like a scientist.

tasks.content: A scientific enquiry project lets you choose your own question to investigate, using the full range of 'working scientifically' skills you have learned, from planning a fair test to collecting, recording and analysing results. You will need to research background information, decide on suitable equipment and a method, and think carefully about how to keep your test fair and safe. Once you have collected your data, you present it clearly in tables and graphs and write a conclusion that answers your original question, evaluating how you could improve your method next time.

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Earth & Space: The Solar System
tasks.content: Our solar system has the Sun at its centre, with eight planets orbiting around it: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The Moon orbits Earth roughly once a month, and its changing appearance from our view is called the lunar phases.

tasks.content: Different animals have different life cycles: a butterfly goes through egg, caterpillar (larva), pupa (chrysalis) and adult butterfly, while a frog goes through egg, tadpole and adult frog - both examples of metamorphosis (a dramatic change in body form). Mammals, like dogs, typically have a simpler life cycle: born as a baby, growing gradually into an adult.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.correctAnswer: A simpler life cycle, born as a baby and growing gradually into an adult

Exactly the same as a butterfly's metamorphosis
No life cycle stages at all

tasks.content: A reversible change can be undone, returning a material to its original state, like melting ice (which can be frozen again) or folding paper (which can be unfolded). An irreversible change cannot easily be undone, like burning paper or baking a cake, since the material has permanently changed into something new.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does a reversible change mean?
questions.correctAnswer: It can be undone, returning the material to its original state
options: It can be undone, returning the material to its original state
It can never be changed at all
It always destroys the material completely
It happens only once and never again

questions.questionText: Give an example of an irreversible change, mentioned in the lesson.

options: The ingredients permanently change into something new that cannot be separated back out

Baking is always a reversible change

questions.correctAnswer: the water can be frozen again, returning the material back to its original solid state

questions.correctAnswer: Burning permanently changes the paper into ash and gases, which cannot be turned back into paper
options: Burning permanently changes the paper into ash and gases, which cannot be turned back into paper
Burnt paper can easily be changed back into its original form

options: They create entirely new substances through a chemical reaction, which cannot simply be reversed back

questions.questionText: Why is understanding reversible and irreversible changes useful in everyday life, like cooking or recycling?

options: It helps explain which materials can be reused or undone, and which cannot, which matters for sustainability and practical tasks

tasks.content: Tamil nouns change their ending, called a vetrumai urubu (வேற்றுமை உருபு), to show their role in a sentence, similar to how English uses word order or prepositions. For example, adding கு (ku) makes a noun a dative case, as in "அவனுக்கு" (avanukku, "to/for him"), while adding ஆல் (aal) makes it instrumental, as in "கையால்" (kaiyaal, "by hand"). Traditional Tamil grammar names eight cases in order: எழுவாய் (nominative), செயப்படுபொருள் (accusative, -ஐ), கருவி (instrumental, -ஆல்), கொடை (dative, -கு), நீங்கல் (ablative, -இல் இருந்து), உடைமை (genitive, -இன்), இடம் (locative, -இல்/கண்) and விளி (vocative). Learning these urubus lets you build precise sentences like "நான் பேனையால் எழுதுகிறேன்" (I write with a pen).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Tamil has two important non-finite verb forms that let you link actions or describe nouns without a full separate sentence. A vinaiyechcham (வினையெச்சம், adverbial participle) shows one action happening before another, like "சாப்பிட்டு படுத்தான்" (saapittu paduthaan, "having eaten, he lay down"), formed by adding -டு/-து to a verb stem. A peyarechcham (பெயரெச்சம், relative/adjectival participle) turns a verb into a word that describes a noun, like "படித்த மாணவன்" (padittha maanavan, "the student who studied", past tense) or "படிக்கும் மாணவன்" (the student who will study/studies, future/habitual). Notice how the peyarechcham always comes directly before the noun it describes, unlike English relative clauses that use "who" or "which".
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The Thirukkural (திருக்குறள்) is a classic Tamil work of 1,330 rhyming couplets (குறள்), traditionally attributed to the poet Thiruvalluvar (திருவள்ளுவர்) and composed roughly 2,000 years ago. It is organised into three major sections called pal (பால்): அறம் (Aram, virtue/ethics, 380 couplets), பொருள் (Porul, wealth and governance) and இன்பம் (Inbam, love). Aram Pal opens with a chapter praising God (கடவுள் வாழ்த்து), and its very first couplet begins "அகர முதல எழுத்தெல்லாம்" (agara mudhala ezhuthellaam), meaning that just as the letter அ (a) is the first of all letters, the eternal one is first in the world. Aram Pal goes on to teach virtues such as honesty, gratitude and kindness for everyday life.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Tamil Kings: The Chola, Pandya & Chera Dynasties
tasks.content: Long ago, ancient Tamil land (Tamilakam) was ruled by three great royal families, often called மூவேந்தர் (the "Three Crowned Kings"): the சோழர் (Chola), பாண்டியர் (Pandya), and சேரர் (Chera). Each dynasty ruled a different region and had its own symbol (emblem). The Cholas ruled the fertile Kaveri river valley in the east, and their emblem was the tiger. Their early capital was Uraiyur. The Pandyas ruled the south, with their capital at மதுரை (Madurai), and their emblem was the fish (carp). Madurai was also a great center of learning, home to the Tamil Sangams — academies of poets who composed and preserved classical Tamil literature. The Cheras ruled the west, in what is now Kerala, with their capital near Vanji, and their emblem was the bow. These three kingdoms sometimes fought each other for power, but they also supported poets, temples, and trade, and their courts are where much of the earliest Tamil literature, called Sangam literature, was composed and collected.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Sangam literature (சங்க இலக்கியம், Sangam Ilakkiyam) is the oldest surviving body of Tamil poetry, traditionally linked to gatherings of poets called sangams said to have met under royal patronage in Madurai. Scholars generally date the surviving poems to roughly the last centuries BCE through the early centuries CE, making it one of the most ancient literatures in India. The poems are organised into two great collections: எட்டுத்தொகை (Ettuthogai, the "Eight Anthologies") and பத்துப்பாட்டு (Pathuppaattu, the "Ten Idylls" or "Ten Songs"). Sangam poetry is traditionally divided by theme into அகம் (agam, poems about inner/personal life such as love) and புறம் (puram, poems about outer/public life such as war, kingship and heroism).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A formal Tamil letter (முறையான கடிதம், muraiyaana kadidham) follows a set structure: it opens with the sender's முகவரி (address) and தேதி (date), followed by a respectful salutation such as "அன்புள்ள ஐயா/அம்மா" (Dear Sir/Madam). The body states its purpose clearly and politely — for example, requesting leave from school might begin "தாழ்மையுடன் தெரிவிப்பது என்னவெனில்" (I humbly wish to inform you that...). It closes with a polite sign-off such as "இங்ஙனம்" (yours truly) or "தங்கள் உண்மையுள்ள" followed by கையொப்பம் (signature) and பெயர் (name). Keeping a formal, respectful tone throughout — avoiding casual spoken-Tamil words — is essential in this kind of writing.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Growing your Tamil vocabulary means learning ஒப்புச்சொல் (oppuchchol, synonyms), எதிர்ச்சொல் (edhirchol, antonyms), and வேர்ச்சொல் (verchol, root words) that connect whole families of related words. For example, "மகிழ்ச்சி" (magizhchi, happiness) shares its meaning with "சந்தோஷம்" (santhosham) — both are synonyms for joy. Antonym pairs include "நல்லது" (good) and "கெட்டது" (bad), or "பெரியது" (big) and "சிறியது" (small). A single root like "படி" (padi, to study/read) grows into a whole word family: "படிப்பு" (padippu, education/study, noun), "படித்தல்" (padithal, the act of reading) and "படிப்பாளி" (padippaali, a scholar) — noticing these shared roots helps you guess the meaning of new words.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A Tamil essay, கட்டுரை (kattturai), follows a clear three-part shape that keeps your ideas organised for the reader. It opens with a முன்னுரை (munnurai, introduction) that presents the topic, moves into a வளர்ச்சி (valarchi, body/development) where you build several paragraphs of supporting ideas and examples, and ends with a முடிவுரை (mudivurai, conclusion) that sums up your main point. For example, an essay titled "சுற்றுச்சூழல் பாதுகாப்பு" (environmental protection) might introduce why the environment matters, develop paragraphs on pollution and solutions, then conclude with a call to action. Planning these three parts before you begin writing helps you stay focused and avoid repeating yourself.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Tamil நாட்டுப்புறப் பாடல்கள் (naattuppura paadalgal, folk songs) were passed down by வாய்மொழி மரபு (oral tradition) long before they were written down, carrying stories, beliefs and daily life across generations by voice alone. A தாலாட்டு (thaalaattu) is a gentle lullaby sung to put a baby to sleep, often repeating soft, soothing sounds. An ஒப்பாரி (oppaari) is a mournful lament sung, often by women, to express grief at a death. கும்மி (kummi) songs are lively, rhythmic songs sung with clapping, traditionally performed by groups of women during festivals, while வில்லுப்பாட்டு (villuppaattu, "bow song") is a dramatic storytelling performance using a bow-shaped instrument as percussion to narrate legends aloud to a village audience.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Strong reading comprehension in Tamil means actively looking for the முக்கிய கருத்து (mukkiya karuthu, main idea) of a passage rather than just recognising individual words. Skilled readers use context clues — the surrounding words and sentences — to work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word instead of stopping to look it up every time. A useful habit is asking the six question words as you read: யார்? (who?), என்ன? (what?), எப்போது? (when?), எங்கே? (where?), ஏன்? (why?) and எப்படி? (how?). levels.levelName: Designing and Writing Programs for a Purpose

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Designing and Writing Programs for a Purpose
tasks.content: Every good program is written to solve a real problem for a real user, so before typing any code or dragging any blocks, a programmer needs to design the solution carefully. Design starts with understanding the purpose: what should the program do, who will use it, and what counts as success? Next comes decomposition, breaking the big problem into smaller, more manageable parts that are each easier to plan and build. For each part, the programmer plans an algorithm, a precise sequence of steps, often sketched first as a flowchart, a storyboard, or written in plain English or pseudocode, before any actual code is written. Planning in this way helps spot problems early, when they are cheap to fix, rather than after a lot of code has already been written. Once the design is clear, the programmer writes the actual program, for example using a block-based language, translating each planned step into real instructions. Good programs also consider the user experience: clear instructions, sensible layouts, and outputs that make sense to the person using them. Finally, the finished program must be tested against its original purpose, checking that it actually does what it was designed to do, using a range of realistic inputs. Designing first and coding second, rather than the other way round, is what separates a well-built program from one that is confusing, unreliable, or does not really solve the problem it was meant to solve.

tasks.content: As programs grow larger, the same set of instructions is often needed more than once, for example resetting a score, moving a sprite in a pattern, or checking a password. Rather than copying the same blocks or lines again and again, programmers group them into a procedure: a named, reusable block of instructions that can be run, or called, whenever it is needed. In many block-based languages this is created as a custom block, sometimes called a 'my block' or a defined block, which appears in the toolbox just like any built-in command once it has been made. Using procedures has several real benefits. It makes programs shorter and easier to read, because the main script becomes a clear list of named actions rather than a long, repeated sequence. It makes programs easier to test and debug, since each procedure can be checked on its own before it is used elsewhere. It also makes programs easier to change, because updating the procedure once automatically updates every place that calls it, instead of needing the same fix repeated many times. Some procedures can also accept inputs, called parameters, so the same procedure can behave slightly differently each time it is called, for example a 'draw shape' procedure that takes the number of sides as a parameter. Learning to spot repeated logic and turn it into a procedure is an important programming skill, closely linked to the idea of abstraction: hiding the detail inside the procedure so the rest of the program can simply use it by name.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Testing and Debugging Larger Programs
tasks.content: As programs become larger and more complex, testing them thoroughly becomes more important, because a single mistake can be hidden among many working parts. Testing means deliberately running a program with a range of inputs to check that it behaves correctly, including normal inputs, extreme inputs, and inputs designed to try to break it. Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors, called bugs, once testing has revealed that something is wrong. There are different kinds of errors to look out for. A syntax error happens when the rules of the language are broken, such as a missing bracket or a block that will not connect properly. A logic error happens when a program runs without crashing but produces the wrong result, because the instructions do not actually do what the programmer intended. A runtime error happens while the program is running, for example if it tries to divide by zero or use a value that does not exist. In larger programs, it helps to test each procedure or section separately before testing the whole program together, since this makes it much easier to narrow down exactly where a problem is coming from. Useful debugging techniques include adding a way to display variable values while the program runs, working through the code slowly step by step, and comparing what the program actually does against what it was designed to do. Careful, systematic testing throughout development, rather than only at the very end, catches problems earlier and makes larger programs far more reliable.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Logical Reasoning: Tracing Program Execution
tasks.content: Tracing a program means carefully working through its instructions one at a time, exactly as a computer would, to predict what it will do without actually running it. This is a vital computational thinking skill because it lets a programmer check their logic on paper, spot mistakes before testing, and understand exactly why a program behaves the way it does. To trace a program, you follow the instructions in order, keeping track of the current value of every variable as it changes, and noting anything the program outputs along the way. A trace table is a useful tool for this: it has a column for each variable and a row for each step, so you can record how the values update as the program runs. For example, if a program starts with a variable called total set to 0, then adds 5, then adds 3, a trace table would show total as 0, then 5, then 8, in three separate rows. Tracing becomes especially important with loops and selection (if statements), since it is easy to misjudge how many times a loop will repeat or which branch of an if statement will run for a given input. Careful tracing also helps identify logic errors: if the traced result does not match what the program was supposed to produce, the mistake can usually be found at the exact step where the values stop making sense. Being able to trace a program accurately, predicting its output before running it, is one of the clearest signs of understanding exactly how a program really works.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Networks and the Internet: How Data Travels

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Networks and the Internet: How Data Travels
tasks.content: A network is simply two or more devices connected together so they can share data and resources, such as files or a printer. A small network in one building, like a home or school, is called a local area network, or LAN. When networks in different, often distant, places are joined together, this is called a wide area network, or WAN. The internet is the largest network of all: a huge, global network of networks, connecting billions of devices around the world. Data does not travel across the internet as one single block. Instead, it is broken up into smaller pieces called packets before it is sent. Each packet is labelled with information including where it has come from and where it needs to go, rather like an address on an envelope. Devices called routers examine this address information and pass each packet along the best available path toward its destination, and different packets belonging to the same piece of data can even take different routes before being reassembled correctly at the other end. This clever system means that if part of a network is busy or unavailable, packets can often still find another way through. To connect to the internet at all, most homes and schools use an internet service provider, or ISP, a company that provides the physical connection and manages the flow of data to and from a wider network. Understanding packets, routers, and how devices are connected together helps explain why the internet is normally so fast and reliable, even when huge numbers of people are using it at once.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Search Technologies: Effective and Critical Use

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Search Technologies: Effective and Critical Use
tasks.content: Search engines let us find information among billions of web pages, but they do not simply store the whole internet and read our minds; they rely on clever technology and need to be used carefully. Behind the scenes, search engines use programs called web crawlers, or spiders, that constantly visit web pages and follow links to find new ones, building a huge index, rather like a giant catalogue, of the words each page contains. When a search is typed in, the search engine does not search the live internet at that moment; instead, it looks through this index and uses a ranking algorithm to decide which pages are most likely to be relevant and trustworthy, based on factors such as how many other reliable sites link to a page and how well it matches the search terms. To search effectively, it helps to choose specific keywords rather than whole sentences, put phrases in quotation marks to search for that exact wording, and use a minus sign to exclude unwanted words from the results. Just as important as searching effectively is thinking critically about the results. Not everything that appears near the top of a search is accurate, unbiased, or up to date, because ranking algorithms measure popularity and relevance, not necessarily truth. Good digital citizens check who wrote a page and why, look for a recent date, compare information across more than one reliable source, and stay alert for adverts or sponsored results that are separate from genuine search results. Searching well is a skill that combines using the technology cleverly with judging its results carefully.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Combining Software for a Real Project

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Combining Software for a Real Project
tasks.content: Real projects, such as producing a school newsletter, a class website, or a campaign presentation, are rarely made using just one piece of software. Instead, they combine several different tools, each chosen because it is well suited to a particular part of the task. A word processor is good for writing and formatting longer pieces of text, a spreadsheet is good for organising numbers, calculations and simple charts, image or drawing software is good for creating or editing pictures, and presentation software is good for building a sequence of slides to show an audience. Combining software effectively means more than just using several programs separately; it means bringing their outputs together into one finished project. This might involve copying a chart created in a spreadsheet and pasting it into a document or a presentation slide, saving an image in a suitable file format so it can be inserted elsewhere, or exporting a document as a PDF so it displays correctly on any device. When work is copied between programs, it is important to check that formatting, image quality and layout still look correct afterwards, since not every file type keeps all of its original formatting when moved. Choosing the right file format also matters: some formats keep quality high but produce very large files, while others compress files to be smaller but may lose some quality. Planning which software to use for each part of a project, and how the different pieces of work will be combined into a single, well-organised final product, is an important computing skill that mirrors how real workplaces produce finished digital documents.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Data Representation: An Introduction to Binary

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Data Representation: An Introduction to Binary
tasks.content: Computers do not understand words, pictures or sounds directly; underneath everything they process, all data is represented using just two digits, 0 and 1, known as binary. This works because a computer's circuits are built from switches that can only be in one of two states, off or on, and these two states are represented by 0 and 1. Each single binary digit is called a bit, short for 'binary digit', and a group of eight bits together is called a byte. Binary numbers work using place value, just like the denary (decimal) numbers we use every day, except each position is worth double the one to its right instead of ten times as much. Reading from the right, the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 for an 8-bit binary number. To convert a binary number to denary, you add together the place values wherever there is a 1. For example, the binary number 00001010 has a 1 in the 8s column and a 1 in the 2s column, so it equals 8 + 2 = 10 in denary. To convert a denary number into binary, you can work out which place values add up to that number: for example, 13 is 8 + 4 + 1, so in binary it is written 00001101. Understanding binary matters because it is the foundation of everything inside a computer: numbers, letters, colours and sounds are all eventually stored and processed as patterns of these two simple digits.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Online Safety: Respectful and Responsible Behaviour

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Online Safety: Respectful and Responsible Behaviour
tasks.content: Using the internet responsibly means treating other people online with the same respect and kindness expected offline, and understanding that actions online have real consequences. Everything shared, posted, liked or commented on adds to a person's digital footprint, a lasting trail of information about them that can be seen by others, including people they never intended to reach, and that can be very difficult to fully remove later. Because of this, it is important to think carefully before posting anything, including photos, comments or personal details, and to remember that private information such as a full name, home address, school, or password should never be shared publicly online. Respectful online behaviour also means being aware of how words can be read differently online than in person, since tone of voice and facial expressions are missing, so a comment intended as a joke can easily be misread as unkind. Cyberbullying, which includes repeated unkind messages, spreading rumours, or excluding someone deliberately online, is a serious issue, and anyone who experiences or witnesses it should tell a trusted adult and use reporting or blocking tools built into apps and websites. It is equally important to be a positive influence, standing up for others rather than joining in with unkind behaviour, and checking before sharing something about whether it might upset or embarrass someone else. Privacy settings on accounts should be reviewed and used sensibly, limiting who can see personal posts and contact the user directly. Being safe and responsible online is an ongoing skill, not a one-off lesson, because technology and the situations it creates keep changing.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Computational thinking is the set of thinking skills that help people solve problems in a logical, structured way, whether or not a computer is involved, and it lies at the heart of everything covered so far this year. The first key skill is decomposition: breaking a large, complicated problem down into smaller parts that are easier to understand, plan and solve individually. The second is pattern recognition: looking for similarities between problems, or within a single problem, so that a solution found once can be reused or adapted elsewhere, rather like noticing that several parts of a program need the same procedure. The third is abstraction: focusing on the important details needed to solve a problem while ignoring information that is not relevant, such as using a simple map instead of a satellite photo, or hiding the detail of a procedure behind a single name. The fourth is algorithm design: creating a precise, ordered set of steps that solves the problem reliably, which can then be tested, traced and, if needed, debugged. These four skills work together throughout the whole process of building a program, from the very first design idea through to writing the code, testing it thoroughly, and fixing any bugs that testing reveals. They also apply well beyond computing, to planning a school project, organising a recipe, or working out the fastest route somewhere. Recognising decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithm design in action, and practising using them together, is what turns programming from following instructions into genuinely solving problems.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In Scratch, a clone is an exact copy of a sprite that appears while your project is running. Instead of dragging out ten identical sprites by hand, you can tell one sprite to make copies of itself using the "create clone of myself" block. This is incredibly useful for games with lots of enemies, raindrops falling from the sky, or bullets flying across the screen. Each clone starts by running its own "when I start as a clone" script, keeps the costume and position of the original sprite at the moment it was created, and can move, change costume, and interact with other sprites completely independently. When a clone is no longer needed, you use "delete this clone" to remove it and free up memory, otherwise your project could slow down or crash if hundreds of clones pile up. A simple example: imagine a "Meteor" sprite. Inside a forever loop, every 2 seconds you run "create clone of myself." Inside "when I start as a clone," the clone goes to a random x position at the top of the screen, then repeats moving down 5 steps until it touches the bottom edge, at which point it deletes itself. This gives you an endless shower of meteors falling down the screen, each one behaving on its own, without you ever having to draw more than one meteor sprite. Clones can also check for collisions, like touching the player sprite, and react by playing a sound or broadcasting a message. Remember that clones are temporary: they disappear when the green flag is clicked again or the project restarts, and any variables you create specifically "for this sprite only" are copied fresh for each clone. Mastering clones lets you build much more dynamic, crowded, and replayable Scratch games with far less manual sprite-building work.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: As your Scratch projects grow bigger, you'll often find yourself repeating the same group of blocks over and over, like a sequence that makes a sprite jump, or one that resets the score to zero. Custom blocks, found under the "My Blocks" category, let you package a whole chunk of code into a single new block with its own name, so you can reuse it anywhere in your project just by dragging it out once. To make one, click "Make a Block," give it a clear name like "jump" or "reset score," then snap the blocks you want it to run underneath the new "define" hat block. From then on, that block appears in your palette and you can drop it into any script. Custom blocks can also take inputs, called parameters, so the block behaves differently each time. For example, you could make a block called "say greeting (name)" where "name" is a text input. Inside the definition, you'd use "say Hello, (name)! for 2 seconds," and every time you use the block you type in a different name, like "Alex" or "Maria," and it greets that specific person. This is exactly how real programmers write functions in text-based languages, so learning custom blocks now builds a habit you'll use for the rest of your coding life. Custom blocks make your project easier to read, because instead of a long messy script, you see short, clearly named blocks like "jump" or "attack enemy." They also make fixing mistakes easier: if you find a bug in how your sprite jumps, you fix it once inside the custom block's definition, and every place that uses "jump" is automatically fixed too. Good programmers always look for repeated code and turn it into a reusable block or function.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Boolean Logic: And, Or, Not
tasks.content: Boolean logic is a way of combining true-or-false statements to make smarter decisions in your code, and Scratch gives you three special operator blocks for it: "and," "or," and "not." A Boolean is simply a value that can only be true or false, like "is the sprite touching the edge?" or "is the score greater than 10?" The "and" block combines two conditions and is only true when BOTH conditions are true. For example, "if touching Player? and key space pressed? then attack" means the attack only happens when the sprite is touching the player AND the space key is pressed at the same time; if either one is false, nothing happens. The "or" block is true when AT LEAST ONE of the two conditions is true. So "if score > 100 or lives = 0 then end game" ends the game if either the score passes 100 or the player runs out of lives, whichever happens first. The "not" block simply flips a condition: it turns true into false and false into true. For example, "if not touching edge? then move 10 steps" means keep moving forward only when you are NOT touching the edge, which is a common way to stop a sprite at the wall. These operators can be combined and nested inside each other to build very precise rules, such as "if not touching Enemy? and key up arrow pressed? then jump," which only lets the sprite jump when it's safe from the enemy and the key is pressed. Learning to read and combine "and," "or," and "not" is one of the most powerful skills in all of coding because every programming language, including Python and JavaScript, uses these exact same three ideas to control decisions.

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Introduction to Algorithms and Flowcharts
tasks.content: An algorithm is simply a clear set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, and you actually use algorithms every day without realizing it, like the steps for brushing your teeth or making a peanut butter sandwich. In coding, an algorithm is the plan you make before you ever touch a single block or line of code. Once you have an algorithm, a great way to picture it visually is with a flowchart, a diagram made of shapes connected by arrows that show the order steps happen in. Flowcharts use a few standard shapes: an oval for the start and end points, a rectangle for an action or instruction, a diamond for a yes/no decision, and arrows to show which step comes next. For example, imagine an algorithm for a sprite deciding whether to jump over an obstacle: Start (oval) leads to an action "check distance to obstacle" (rectangle), which leads to a decision diamond "is obstacle close?" If the answer is yes, an arrow leads to the action "jump"; if no, an arrow leads to "keep walking." Both paths then lead back around to "check distance to obstacle" again, showing this repeats in a loop, until eventually reaching an End oval. Flowcharts are valuable because they let you plan and spot problems in your logic before you build anything, saving time and preventing bugs. They also make it easy to share your idea with a partner or explain it to someone else, since diagrams are often easier to follow at a glance than a wall of code. Every program you will ever write, whether in Scratch, Python, or any other language, starts life as an algorithm, and being able to sketch that algorithm as a flowchart is a skill professional software engineers use constantly when planning real applications.

levels.levelName: Pseudocode: Writing Code in Plain English

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Pseudocode: Writing Code in Plain English
tasks.content: Pseudocode is a way of writing out the logic of a program using plain, everyday language instead of the exact symbols and syntax of a real programming language. It is not meant to run on a computer; it is meant to help you, the programmer, think clearly and plan before you write actual code in Scratch, Python, or anything else. Because pseudocode doesn't follow strict rules, you have freedom in how you write it, but good pseudocode is still organized, using indentation and clear action words like "set," "if," "repeat," and "print" so that the logic is easy to follow. For example, here is pseudocode for a simple guessing game: START, set secretNumber to 7, repeat: ask the player to guess a number, if guess equals secretNumber then print "You win!" and stop, else if guess is less than secretNumber then print "Too low," else print "Too high," END repeat when correct. Notice this reads almost like a story, but it still captures every decision and every repeat exactly like a real program would need. Writing pseudocode first is incredibly useful because it separates two different jobs: figuring out WHAT your program needs to do, and figuring out HOW to write it in a specific language's exact syntax. When you try to do both at once, it's easy to get stuck or confused. Once your pseudocode logic makes sense and covers every situation, like what happens if the guess is right, too high, or too low, translating it into Scratch blocks or Python code becomes much simpler, because you already know exactly what each part needs to do. Professional software developers write pseudocode or similar planning notes all the time before tackling a tricky piece of a real program, especially for algorithms with lots of decisions and repeated steps.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Working with Lists in Scratch
tasks.content: A list in Scratch is a way to store many pieces of information under one single name, instead of creating a separate variable for every item. Imagine you want to keep track of the top 5 high scores in a game; making five separate variables called score1, score2, and so on would be messy and hard to work with. Instead, you create one list called "High Scores," and it can hold as many items as you need, growing or shrinking while the project runs. To make a list, go to the Variables category and click "Make a List." Once created, you get blocks like "add (thing) to (list)" to put a new item at the end, "delete (item) of (list)" to remove one, "item (1) of (list)" to look up what's stored at a specific position (called an index), and "length of (list)" to find out how many items it holds. For example, if you have a list called "Names" and use "add Maria to Names," then "add Alex to Names," the list now contains two items: Maria at position 1 and Alex at position 2. Using "item 1 of Names" would report back "Maria." Lists are perfect for things like a shopping list game, storing everyone's guesses in a quiz, tracking an inventory of items a character has collected, or holding a sequence of words to build a sentence randomly. You can also combine lists with loops: using a "repeat" block with "item (i) of (list)," where i changes each time, lets you go through every single item in a list one by one, printing it, checking it, or changing it. This idea of stepping through a list item by item is so important that it appears in every programming language, usually called a "for each" loop, so getting comfortable with Scratch lists now will make lists in Python feel very familiar later.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Randomness is what makes games feel fresh and unpredictable every time you play them, and Scratch gives you an easy tool for it: the "pick random () to ()" block, found in the Operators category. This block reports a random whole number between the two values you type in, including both endpoints. For example, "pick random 1 to 6" simulates rolling a six-sided die, giving you a 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6, each time with an equal chance, just like real dice. Random numbers are useful for far more than dice games. You could use "pick random -200 to 200" to place a sprite at a random x position on the stage, making enemies appear in different spots each time you play. You could use "pick random 1 to 3" combined with an "if / else if / else" chain to make a sprite randomly choose one of three costumes, so it looks different every time your project starts. You can even combine random numbers with lists: use "pick random 1 to (length of list)" as the index inside "item () of (list)" to randomly select an item from a list of jokes, quiz questions, or prizes. A common project idea is a "Magic 8 Ball," where a list holds several possible answers like "Yes," "No," and "Ask again later," and clicking the sprite picks a random index from that list and says the answer out loud. It's important to understand that "pick random" in Scratch includes both numbers you type, so "pick random 1 to 10" can actually produce a 1 or a 10, not just the numbers in between. Learning to use randomness well, mixing it with variables, lists, and conditionals, is what turns a predictable, boring project into a game that feels new and exciting every single time someone plays it.

tasks.content: As Scratch projects grow bigger, with more sprites, more custom blocks, clones, and variables, bugs become harder to find just by staring at the code. Debugging is the skill of finding and fixing problems in a program, and experienced coders use a set of reliable strategies rather than guessing randomly. The first strategy is isolating the problem: instead of testing your entire game at once, click just the script that seems broken, or temporarily disconnect other scripts, to narrow down exactly which block is misbehaving. The second is using "say" or "think" blocks as checkpoints, having a sprite say the current value of a variable, like "say (score)," at different points in your script, so you can watch how that value changes as the project runs and spot exactly where it goes wrong. Scratch's built-in variable checkbox, which displays a variable's live value on the stage, works the same way and is often faster to set up. A third strategy is checking your logic order: many bugs happen because blocks run in the wrong sequence, such as checking "if score > 10" before the score actually gets updated that frame, so tracing through your script step by step, block by block, exactly as the computer would, often reveals the issue. A fourth strategy, especially useful with clones and custom blocks, is testing in isolation: build a small, separate test script that only creates one clone or calls one custom block, so you can watch its behavior without a busy, crowded project distracting you. Common bugs in bigger projects include forgetting to reset a variable at the start, using "broadcast" without the matching "when I receive," or comparing text and numbers incorrectly. The most important debugging habit of all is patience: read your code slowly and literally, one block at a time, assuming the computer is doing exactly what you told it, not what you meant.
Let's practice what we just learned!
