tasks.content: A persuasive speech uses techniques like the rule of three (grouping ideas in threes for impact, 'education, opportunity, hope'), direct address (speaking to 'you' the audience), emotive language (words that stir feelings), and repetition to drive a point home. Unlike written persuasion, a speech also relies on tone of voice, pace, and pauses for emphasis when delivered aloud.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What is the 'rule of three'?
questions.correctAnswer: Grouping ideas in threes for impact
options: Grouping ideas in threes for impact

questions.questionText: What technique speaks directly to the audience using 'you'?
What is emotive language designed to do?
Besides word choice, what else matters when delivering a speech aloud?
Why might a speaker pause before a key point?
questions.correctAnswer: To create emphasis and let it sink in
options: To create emphasis and let it sink in

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Give an example of the rule of three applied to a slogan (three linked words/ideas).
Why is repetition powerful in a speech?
questions.correctAnswer: It reinforces the key message so the audience remembers it
options: It reinforces the key message so the audience remembers it

questions.questionText: What is the term for language chosen to trigger an emotional response?
How does a speech differ from a persuasive essay in delivery?
questions.correctAnswer: It relies on tone, pace and pauses
options: It relies on tone, pace and pauses

questions.questionText: What technique makes an audience feel personally spoken to?
Which best shows the rule of three?
questions.correctAnswer: We will fight, we will win, we will succeed.
options: We will fight, we will win, we will succeed.

tasks.content: Non-fiction texts include articles, biographies, and reports, each written for a specific audience and purpose. When analysing non-fiction, consider the writer's viewpoint (are they neutral or biased?), the evidence used (facts, statistics, expert opinions), and features like headings, subheadings and bullet points that help organise information for the reader.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What might indicate a non-fiction writer is biased?
questions.correctAnswer: They only present one side, favourably
options: They only present one side, favourably

questions.questionText: Name one type of evidence a non-fiction writer might use to support a claim.
What is the purpose of subheadings in a non-fiction text?
questions.correctAnswer: To organise information for the reader
options: To organise information for the reader

questions.questionText: What word describes writing that presents information fairly, without favouring one side?
Why is it important to consider a writer's purpose when analysing non-fiction?
questions.correctAnswer: It helps explain their choices of content and tone
options: It helps explain their choices of content and tone
All non-fiction has the same purpose

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Name one non-fiction text type, besides an article or biography.
questions.correctAnswer: report (or a speech transcript, letter, etc.)

questions.questionText: What might a biased text look like?
questions.correctAnswer: Only positive facts about one side of an argument
options: Only positive facts about one side of an argument

questions.questionText: What text feature breaks information into a quick, scannable list?
Why might a writer include statistics in a non-fiction piece?
questions.correctAnswer: To support their claims with evidence
options: To support their claims with evidence

questions.questionText: What do we call the intended readers of a text?
Which of these is a sign of an objective (unbiased) text?

tasks.content: William Shakespeare wrote plays and poems in the late 1500s and early 1600s, and his work still influences English today - many common phrases, like 'break the ice' and 'wild goose chase', come from his plays. Shakespeare wrote in a mix of prose and verse, often iambic pentameter (a rhythm of five stressed-unstressed beats per line), and his plays are grouped into comedies, tragedies and histories.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: In roughly what period did Shakespeare write his plays?
Name one of the three main categories Shakespeare's plays are grouped into (comedy, tragedy, or ___).
What is iambic pentameter?
questions.correctAnswer: A rhythm of five stressed-unstressed beats per line
options: A type of rhyme scheme only
A rhythm of five stressed-unstressed beats per line

questions.questionText: Give one modern phrase that originally comes from Shakespeare.
questions.correctAnswer: break the ice (or wild goose chase, etc.)

questions.questionText: What two forms did Shakespeare mix in his writing?

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Name one of the three main categories Shakespeare's plays are grouped into, besides history.
Why is iambic pentameter significant in Shakespeare's plays?
questions.correctAnswer: It gives the verse a natural, rhythmic beat
options: It gives the verse a natural, rhythmic beat
It is only used in comedies

questions.questionText: What do we call the type of writing that doesn't follow a strict rhythmic pattern, unlike verse?
How has Shakespeare influenced modern English?
questions.correctAnswer: Many everyday phrases come from his plays
options: Many everyday phrases come from his plays
He only affected poetry, not speech

questions.questionText: What type of Shakespeare play usually ends happily, often with a marriage?
What type of Shakespeare play usually ends in death or downfall for the main character?

tasks.content: Dialogue (characters' spoken words) reveals personality, relationships and emotion without the narrator stating it directly. How a character speaks - their word choice, sentence length, even what they don't say - tells us about who they are. Analysing dialogue means looking closely at these choices to understand character and tension in a scene.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What can dialogue reveal about a character?
options: Only the time period of the story

questions.questionText: What might a character's word choice in dialogue reveal?
Why might analysing what a character does NOT say be useful?
questions.correctAnswer: Silence or avoidance can reveal hidden feelings or tension
options: Silence or avoidance can reveal hidden feelings or tension
Analysing silence has no literary value

questions.questionText: What does analysing dialogue help you understand, besides character?
How does dialogue differ from narration in revealing character?
questions.correctAnswer: Dialogue shows character indirectly, through speech, rather than direct narrator description
options: Dialogue shows character indirectly, through speech, rather than direct narrator description
They are exactly the same technique
Dialogue is always less revealing than narration

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: What might short, clipped dialogue suggest about a character's emotional state?
Why might a writer give two characters very different speech patterns?
questions.correctAnswer: To distinguish their personalities and backgrounds clearly
options: To distinguish their personalities and backgrounds clearly
Speech patterns never differ between characters

questions.questionText: What literary skill involves closely examining a character's spoken words for deeper meaning?
Which best shows how dialogue can reveal relationships between characters?
questions.correctAnswer: The way characters address or interrupt each other
options: The way characters address or interrupt each other
Only the narrator can show relationships
Only actions reveal relationships, not speech

questions.questionText: Why might a reader pay attention to interruptions or pauses within dialogue?
questions.correctAnswer: they can signal tension, hesitation or power dynamics between characters

questions.questionText: Which best summarises why dialogue analysis matters in fiction study?
questions.correctAnswer: It reveals character and tension indirectly, without explicit narration
options: It reveals character and tension indirectly, without explicit narration
Only narration should ever be analysed
Dialogue only matters for comedic effect

tasks.content: Tone is the writer's attitude towards their subject (serious, humorous, sarcastic), while register is how formal or informal the language is, chosen to suit the audience and purpose. A text message uses a casual register, while a job application uses a formal one - mismatching tone or register with a situation can seem inappropriate or confusing.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does 'tone' refer to in writing?
questions.correctAnswer: The writer's attitude towards their subject
options: The writer's attitude towards their subject

questions.questionText: What does 'register' refer to in writing?
questions.correctAnswer: how formal or informal the language is

questions.questionText: Which register would a text message to a friend typically use?
Which register would a job application typically use?
What might happen if tone or register doesn't match the situation?
questions.correctAnswer: It could seem inappropriate or confusing
options: It could seem inappropriate or confusing
Readers never notice tone or register

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Give an example of a tone a writer might use, besides serious.
Which factor should influence the register a writer chooses?
questions.correctAnswer: The audience and purpose of the writing
options: The audience and purpose of the writing
The time of day it's written

questions.questionText: What might a sarcastic tone suggest the writer actually means, compared to their literal words?
questions.correctAnswer: the opposite of what is literally stated

questions.questionText: Which best distinguishes tone from register?
questions.correctAnswer: Tone is attitude; register is level of formality
options: Tone is attitude; register is level of formality
Register is attitude; tone is formality

questions.questionText: Why might a writer deliberately use a humorous tone for a serious topic?
questions.correctAnswer: to engage readers or soften a difficult subject (varies by purpose)

questions.questionText: Why is understanding tone and register an important reading skill?
questions.correctAnswer: It helps readers correctly interpret a writer's intended attitude and appropriateness
options: It helps readers correctly interpret a writer's intended attitude and appropriateness
Tone and register have no effect on meaning
These concepts only apply to spoken language

tasks.content: A review gives an opinion on a book or film, supported by specific reasons and examples, not just 'I liked it' or 'it was boring'. A good review usually includes a brief summary (without spoiling the ending), discussion of specific strengths and weaknesses, and a clear overall recommendation or rating for the reader.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What should a review be supported by, rather than just a vague opinion?
options: Only the title of the book/film

questions.questionText: What should a review's summary avoid doing to the ending?
What should a good review discuss, besides a summary?
options: Only the price of the ticket/book

questions.questionText: What should a review usually end with?
questions.correctAnswer: a clear overall recommendation or rating

questions.questionText: Why is 'I liked it' considered a weak review on its own?
questions.correctAnswer: It gives no specific reasons or evidence to support the opinion
options: It gives no specific reasons or evidence to support the opinion
It is always a complete and sufficient review
Short opinions are always the strongest reviews

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why might a reviewer avoid revealing major plot twists?
questions.correctAnswer: to avoid spoiling the story for readers who haven't experienced it yet

questions.questionText: Which is a specific, well-supported review statement?
questions.correctAnswer: The pacing dragged in the middle because too many scenes repeated the same conflict.
options: The pacing dragged in the middle because too many scenes repeated the same conflict.

questions.questionText: What might a review's 'weaknesses' section discuss?
questions.correctAnswer: parts of the book/film that didn't work well

questions.questionText: Why is a clear recommendation useful at the end of a review?
questions.correctAnswer: It helps the reader quickly decide whether to watch/read it
options: It helps the reader quickly decide whether to watch/read it
Reviews should never give a final opinion
Only the summary matters, not the recommendation

questions.questionText: What balance should a fair review try to include, besides only positives?
Which best summarises what makes a review genuinely useful to readers?
questions.correctAnswer: Specific, balanced, well-supported opinions with a clear recommendation
options: Specific, balanced, well-supported opinions with a clear recommendation
A one-word opinion with no explanation
A full retelling of the entire plot

tasks.content: A typical story structure includes exposition (introducing characters and setting), rising action (building tension through events), climax (the most intense turning point), falling action (events after the climax) and resolution (how the story concludes). Understanding this structure helps writers plan a story that builds and resolves tension effectively.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What happens in the exposition of a story?
What is the most intense turning point of a story called?
What happens during the rising action?
options: The story is introduced for the first time

questions.questionText: What is the final part of a typical story structure, where things conclude, called?
What happens during the falling action?
questions.correctAnswer: Events that happen after the climax
options: Events that happen after the climax
The introduction of new unrelated characters only

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Put these story structure stages in order: resolution, climax, exposition, rising action, falling action.
questions.correctAnswer: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution

questions.questionText: Why is the exposition an important part of a story's structure?
questions.correctAnswer: It establishes the characters and setting the rest of the story depends on
options: It establishes the characters and setting the rest of the story depends on
It has no real purpose in a story
It always comes after the climax
Only the climax matters in a story

questions.questionText: Why might a writer build 'rising action' gradually rather than jumping straight to the climax?
questions.correctAnswer: to build tension and keep the reader engaged before the most intense moment

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of the resolution in a story?
questions.correctAnswer: To show how the conflicts or tension from earlier are concluded
options: To show how the conflicts or tension from earlier are concluded
To introduce brand new unrelated conflicts

questions.questionText: Why might understanding story structure help a writer plan a story in advance?
questions.correctAnswer: it helps them map out how and when tension should build and resolve throughout the story

questions.questionText: Why might a story feel unsatisfying if it skips straight from exposition to resolution?
questions.correctAnswer: Without rising action and a climax, there is no build-up of tension for the resolution to pay off
options: Without rising action and a climax, there is no build-up of tension for the resolution to pay off
Skipping those stages always improves a story
Rising action and climax are never actually necessary
A story's structure has no effect on how satisfying it feels

tasks.content: Character development refers to how a character changes or grows over the course of a story, often as a result of the events and challenges they face. Writers show character development through a character's actions, dialogue, and how other characters react to them, rather than simply telling the reader directly that the character has changed.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does character development refer to?
questions.correctAnswer: How a character changes or grows over the course of a story
options: How a character changes or grows over the course of a story

questions.questionText: What often causes a character to develop or change in a story?
questions.correctAnswer: the events and challenges they face

questions.questionText: How do writers usually show character development?
questions.correctAnswer: Through actions, dialogue, and other characters' reactions
options: Through actions, dialogue, and other characters' reactions
By directly telling the reader the character has changed, with no other evidence
Character development is never actually shown
Only through the character's physical appearance

questions.questionText: Why might a writer prefer to SHOW character development rather than just telling the reader about it?
questions.correctAnswer: showing is often more engaging and convincing than simply stating a fact

questions.questionText: What might a shy character's development into a braver character be shown through?
questions.correctAnswer: Their changing actions and dialogue throughout the story
options: Their changing actions and dialogue throughout the story
Just the narrator stating 'he became brave'
Character development cannot be shown this way

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Give an example of how a character's dialogue might show they have become more confident.
questions.correctAnswer: e.g. speaking up more, challenging others, or expressing opinions directly

questions.questionText: Why is 'showing, not telling' considered a stronger technique for character development?
questions.correctAnswer: It lets readers infer and experience the change themselves, making it feel more real
options: It lets readers infer and experience the change themselves, making it feel more real
Telling the reader directly is always more convincing
Showing has no advantage over telling
Character development should never be demonstrated through action

questions.questionText: Why might how OTHER characters react to a character help show that character's development?
questions.correctAnswer: their reactions can reflect how the character's behaviour or attitude has visibly changed

questions.questionText: Why might an author use a flashback to show a character's past before their development?
questions.correctAnswer: To give the reader a clear contrast between who the character was and who they've become
options: To give the reader a clear contrast between who the character was and who they've become
Flashbacks never relate to character development
Only the present moment matters for character analysis
Flashbacks always confuse the reader with no benefit

questions.questionText: Why might a character's internal thoughts (if shown) reveal character development that their actions alone do not?
questions.correctAnswer: internal thoughts can reveal a change in feelings or beliefs that isn't always visible from the outside

questions.questionText: Why is analysing character development an important skill when studying literature?
questions.correctAnswer: It helps readers understand the deeper themes and messages the author is exploring through that character
options: It helps readers understand the deeper themes and messages the author is exploring through that character
Character development has no connection to a story's themes
Only a character's name matters in literary analysis
Development analysis is not useful for understanding literature

tasks.content: A persuasive speech is written to be spoken aloud, convincing an audience of a particular viewpoint, often opening with a strong hook to grab attention, followed by clear arguments supported by evidence, and ending with a memorable call to action. Unlike persuasive writing on a page, a speech also considers tone of voice, pace and pauses for effect.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What is a persuasive speech written to do?
questions.correctAnswer: Be spoken aloud, convincing an audience of a viewpoint
options: Be spoken aloud, convincing an audience of a viewpoint
Describe a scene with no argument
List unrelated facts with no persuasion

questions.questionText: What does a persuasive speech often open with, to grab attention?
What should a speech's arguments be supported by?
What does a persuasive speech often end with?
What does a speech consider that persuasive writing on a page does not need to?
questions.correctAnswer: Tone of voice, pace and pauses
options: Tone of voice, pace and pauses

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Give an example of a strong opening hook for a speech about protecting the environment.
questions.correctAnswer: e.g. a striking fact, question, or story about environmental damage

questions.questionText: Why might a speaker pause before delivering their most important point?
questions.correctAnswer: A pause can build anticipation and emphasise the importance of what follows
options: A pause can build anticipation and emphasise the importance of what follows
Pauses have no effect on how a speech is received
Pausing always weakens a speech's impact
Speeches should never include any pauses

questions.questionText: Why is a 'call to action' an effective way to end a persuasive speech?
questions.correctAnswer: it tells the audience exactly what to do next, turning their agreement into action

questions.questionText: Why might varying your pace (speaking faster or slower) be effective in a speech?
questions.correctAnswer: It can build excitement or create emphasis on key points
options: It can build excitement or create emphasis on key points
Pace should always stay exactly the same throughout a speech
Varying pace always confuses the audience
Pace has no effect on a speech's impact

questions.questionText: Why might a speechwriter choose simpler, clearer sentences than they would use in written persuasive text?
questions.correctAnswer: a listening audience can't re-read a sentence, so spoken language usually needs to be easier to follow instantly

questions.questionText: Why is a memorable call to action important at the end of a persuasive speech?
questions.correctAnswer: It gives the audience a clear, lasting message about what they should do after hearing the speech
options: It gives the audience a clear, lasting message about what they should do after hearing the speech
Speeches don't need a clear ending
A call to action always confuses an audience
Endings have no effect on how persuasive a speech feels

tasks.content: Symbolism is when an object, colour, or image represents a deeper idea beyond its literal meaning - a storm might symbolise inner turmoil, or a wilting flower might symbolise lost hope. Recognising symbolism helps readers understand the deeper themes an author is exploring, beyond just the literal events of the story.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What is symbolism?
questions.correctAnswer: When an object, colour, or image represents a deeper idea beyond its literal meaning
options: When an object, colour, or image represents a deeper idea beyond its literal meaning
When words only ever mean their literal meaning

questions.questionText: What might a storm symbolise, according to the lesson?
What might a wilting flower symbolise?
options: A literal flower with no deeper meaning

questions.questionText: What does recognising symbolism help readers understand?
questions.correctAnswer: the deeper themes an author is exploring

questions.questionText: What is symbolism beyond, according to the lesson?
questions.correctAnswer: The literal events of the story
options: The literal events of the story
Nothing beyond the literal story at all

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why might a storm in a story symbolise a character's inner turmoil, rather than just describing the weather?
questions.correctAnswer: a storm's chaos and intensity can mirror the emotional conflict or unrest a character is experiencing inside

questions.questionText: Why might an author use a wilting flower to symbolise lost hope, instead of directly stating 'the character lost hope'?

options: A symbolic image can convey the idea more subtly and powerfully, letting the reader interpret and feel the meaning themselves
Symbolism never actually adds anything beyond a direct statement
Directly stating an idea is always more effective than symbolism
A wilting flower has no possible symbolic connection to hope

questions.questionText: Why might the same symbol, like a storm, mean something different in two different stories?
questions.correctAnswer: the meaning of a symbol depends on its context within a specific story, not a single universal definition

questions.questionText: Why does recognising symbolism require looking beyond the literal events of a story?
questions.correctAnswer: Symbolism operates on a deeper level of meaning that isn't stated directly, so understanding it means interpreting beyond just what literally happens
options: Symbolism operates on a deeper level of meaning that isn't stated directly, so understanding it means interpreting beyond just what literally happens
Symbolism is always stated directly and literally in the text
Looking at literal events alone always reveals every symbol
Symbolism has no connection to deeper meaning at all

questions.questionText: Why might recognising symbolism deepen a reader's appreciation of a story's themes?
questions.correctAnswer: it reveals additional layers of meaning the author has woven into the story, beyond just the surface-level plot

questions.questionText: Why is symbolism considered an important literary device to study at this level?

Symbolism has no real importance in studying literature
Authors never actually use symbolism in their writing

tasks.content: Preparing for a debate means researching your topic thoroughly, developing strong arguments with evidence, and anticipating counterarguments the other side might raise so you can respond to them. Good debaters also practise clear, confident delivery, since how you present an argument matters alongside the argument itself.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does preparing for a debate involve, besides researching your topic?
options: Only memorising random facts with no structure

questions.questionText: What should good debate preparation help you anticipate?
questions.correctAnswer: counterarguments the other side might raise

questions.questionText: Why should you anticipate counterarguments?
questions.correctAnswer: So you can respond to them
options: So you can respond to them
So you can ignore them completely
Counterarguments never need to be considered
To avoid your own argument entirely

questions.questionText: What should good debaters practise, besides their arguments?
Why does delivery matter alongside the argument itself?
questions.correctAnswer: How you present an argument affects how convincing it is to an audience
options: How you present an argument affects how convincing it is to an audience
Delivery has no effect on how convincing an argument is
Only the words used ever matter in a debate
Confidence has no connection to persuasiveness

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why is thorough research an essential first step in preparing for a debate?
questions.correctAnswer: well-researched facts and evidence give your arguments credibility and make them harder for the opposing side to challenge

questions.questionText: Why might anticipating the other side's strongest counterargument be more useful than only preparing your own points?

Only your own side's points ever matter in a debate
Anticipating challenges has no real benefit in debate preparation

questions.questionText: Why might practising confident delivery help even a well-researched argument land more effectively?

questions.questionText: Why might a debater use evidence, like statistics or expert opinions, rather than just personal opinion, to support their argument?
questions.correctAnswer: Evidence adds objective credibility to an argument, making it more convincing than opinion alone
options: Evidence adds objective credibility to an argument, making it more convincing than opinion alone
Personal opinion is always more convincing than evidence in a debate
Evidence has no real role in strengthening a debate argument
Debates are never actually won using evidence

questions.questionText: Why might debaters prepare rebuttals (responses) in advance, rather than only thinking of them during the debate itself?

questions.questionText: Why is learning to prepare for a debate a valuable skill beyond the debate itself?

options: It builds research, critical thinking, and persuasive communication skills that are useful in many other academic and real-world situations
Debate preparation skills have no use outside of a formal debate
This skill is only ever relevant within a single debate activity
Critical thinking has no connection to debate preparation

tasks.content: An autobiographical piece is written by the author about their own life, in first person, often focusing on a specific meaningful event or period rather than trying to cover everything. Good autobiographical writing includes personal reflection - not just what happened, but what the writer learned or how it changed them.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: Who writes an autobiographical piece, about whose life?

options: The author, about their own life
A stranger, about someone else's life
Nobody - it's always a made-up story
A historian, about a historical figure

questions.questionText: What point of view is an autobiographical piece written in?
What does good autobiographical writing often focus on?
questions.correctAnswer: A specific meaningful event or period, rather than everything
options: A specific meaningful event or period, rather than everything
Every single detail of an entire life
Someone else's life instead of the author's own

questions.questionText: What should good autobiographical writing include, besides what happened?
questions.correctAnswer: personal reflection on what was learned or how it changed the writer

questions.questionText: What makes autobiographical writing different from just a list of life events?
questions.correctAnswer: It includes personal reflection on what was learned or how it changed the writer
options: It includes personal reflection on what was learned or how it changed the writer
It never includes any personal reflection
It is always written by someone else
A list of events is always more meaningful than reflection

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why might an autobiographical piece focus on one specific meaningful event, rather than trying to summarise an entire life?
questions.correctAnswer: focusing on one event allows for deeper, more meaningful reflection than a shallow overview of everything, which wouldn't give the same insight

questions.questionText: Why is personal reflection considered an essential part of autobiographical writing, not just reporting what happened?
questions.correctAnswer: Reflection reveals the deeper meaning or personal growth from an experience, which is what makes autobiographical writing insightful rather than just a factual account
options: Reflection reveals the deeper meaning or personal growth from an experience, which is what makes autobiographical writing insightful rather than just a factual account
Reflection has no real place in autobiographical writing

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Ratio, Proportion & Rates of Change
tasks.content: Two quantities are in direct proportion if their ratio stays constant, so if y = kx and we know one pair of values we can find k and use it to find others. Two quantities are in inverse proportion if one increases as the other decreases, so xy = k stays constant. For example, if y is directly proportional to x and y = 12 when x = 4, then k = 3, so when x = 9, y = 27.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In a right-angled triangle, Pythagoras' theorem states that a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle). To find the hypotenuse, square both shorter sides, add them, then square root: legs of 3 and 4 give a hypotenuse of the square root of (9 + 16) = the square root of 25 = 5. To find a shorter side, rearrange: square the hypotenuse, subtract the known side squared, then square root.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A scatter graph shows the relationship between two variables using plotted points. If the points generally rise from left to right, this is positive correlation (both variables increase together); if they generally fall, this is negative correlation; if there is no clear pattern, there is no correlation. A line of best fit can be used to estimate values and make predictions: for a line y = 2x + 3, when x = 6, y = 15.

For example, the probability of flipping a head then rolling a 6 is 1/2 x 1/6 = 1/12. Tree diagrams and sample space diagrams help organise combined outcomes, such as the 36 possible outcomes when rolling two dice.

tasks.content: Two quantities are in direct proportion if they increase or decrease at the same rate - if y is directly proportional to x, then y = kx for some constant k, and doubling x doubles y. Two quantities are in inverse proportion if one increases as the other decreases, following y = k/x, so doubling x halves y. A classic example: the more workers on a job (direct relationship with speed), the less time it takes - but the time and number of workers are in inverse proportion.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Two shapes are congruent if they are exactly the same size and shape - one could be rotated, reflected or moved on top of the other and match perfectly. Two shapes are similar if they are the same shape but different sizes, meaning one is an enlargement of the other with all angles equal and sides in the same ratio (scale factor). If a shape is enlarged by scale factor 2, every side doubles in length, but the angles stay exactly the same.

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorising
tasks.content: A quadratic equation has the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0. To solve by factorising, find two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b, then write the equation as two brackets. For example, x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0 factorises to (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0, so x = -2 or x = -3. Once factorised, each bracket can be set equal to zero separately to find the solutions, since anything multiplied by zero equals zero.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Finding the nth Term of Linear Sequences
tasks.content: The nth term of a linear sequence is a formula that lets you find any term without listing them all. For the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15 (adding 4 each time), the nth term is 4n - 1: check n=1 gives 4(1)-1=3, correct. The number added each time becomes the coefficient of n, and you then adjust with a constant to match the first term.

Digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing and saliva start to break down food, continues in the stomach with acid and enzymes, and is completed in the small intestine, where enzymes finish breaking down food and nutrients are absorbed through finger-like projections called villi. Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up digestion: amylase breaks down starch into sugars, protease breaks down proteins into amino acids, and lipase breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

Many reactions involve an energy change: exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, often as heat, causing the temperature to rise, while endothermic reactions absorb energy, causing the temperature to fall. Chemical reactions can be represented using word equations and balanced symbol equations, which show exactly how many atoms of each element are involved on both sides.

tasks.content: Electric current is the flow of electrical charge around a circuit, measured in amperes (amps, A) with an ammeter, while voltage (potential difference), measured in volts with a voltmeter, is the energy transferred per unit of charge that pushes the current around. Magnets have two poles, north and south, and like poles repel while opposite poles attract, with the invisible magnetic field around a magnet mapped using field lines that run from north to south. An electric current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field around it, and this effect, called electromagnetism, is used to make electromagnets, which are magnets that can be switched on and off using electricity.

tasks.content: An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms (the community) in an area interacting with each other and with the non-living parts of their environment, such as soil, water and climate. Within an ecosystem, organisms depend on one another through feeding relationships shown in food chains and food webs, where energy passes from producers (usually plants, which make their own food by photosynthesis) to primary consumers, then secondary and tertiary consumers. This interdependence means that a change affecting one species, such as a predator being removed, can have knock-on effects throughout the whole food web, which is why maintaining balanced ecosystems is important.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The periodic table arranges all known elements in order of increasing atomic number, into rows called periods and columns called groups, with elements in the same group sharing similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. Metals, found on the left and centre of the table, are typically shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, and malleable, while non-metals, found on the right, are generally dull, brittle if solid, and poor conductors. Group 1 elements, the alkali metals, are very reactive and get more reactive down the group, while Group 0, the noble gases, are extremely unreactive because they already have full outer electron shells.

Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when burned, contributing to climate change, while most renewable resources produce little or no carbon dioxide during use but can be less reliable, such as solar power depending on sunlight. Choosing energy resources involves weighing up factors like cost, reliability, environmental impact and how much energy each resource can supply.

tasks.content: Light and sound both travel as waves, but light is a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum (such as space) at very high speed, while sound is a longitudinal wave caused by vibrations, which needs a medium like air, water or a solid to travel through, and travels much more slowly. Waves are described using amplitude (the maximum displacement, related to loudness for sound or brightness for light), wavelength (the distance between two matching points on a wave), and frequency (the number of waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz), linked by the wave equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength. Higher frequency sound waves are heard as higher pitch, while for light, higher frequency corresponds to a different colour, towards the violet/blue end of the visible spectrum.

tasks.content: Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity, called the reactivity series, which helps predict how they will behave in reactions: more reactive metals, such as potassium and sodium, react vigorously, while less reactive metals, such as gold and copper, are largely unreactive. Many metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas (more readily for reactive metals), and react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound in a displacement reaction, which is further evidence used to build up the reactivity series.

tasks.content: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food, using energy from light to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen; it takes place mainly in the chloroplasts of leaf cells, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy. Respiration, in contrast, occurs in all living cells and releases energy from glucose for the organism to use; aerobic respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, while anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and, in animal cells, produces lactic acid instead. Photosynthesis and respiration are essentially opposite processes, and together they play a key role in maintaining the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

tasks.content: Evaluating an investigation means critically reviewing how well the method worked and how confident you can be in the results, rather than simply describing what was done. This includes identifying sources of error, such as random errors (small, unpredictable variations, reduced by repeating measurements and averaging) and systematic errors (a consistent bias, often caused by a fault in equipment such as an incorrectly zeroed balance, which shifts every reading in the same direction). A good evaluation also considers the investigation's reliability (whether repeating it gives consistent results) and validity (whether it actually tests what it claims to, with all other variables properly controlled), and suggests specific, practical improvements.

tasks.content: A chemical reaction happens when substances (reactants) change into new substances (products), often shown using a chemical equation, like hydrogen + oxygen -> water. tasks.content: Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter itself - like how a sound wave moves through air, or a wave moves across the surface of water. Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: புணர்ச்சி (puṇarcci, sandhi) refers to the rules governing how sounds change when two words are joined together in Tamil, similar to how English "do not" becomes "don't." A common example is "மழை" (mazhai, rain) combining with "காலம்" (kaalam, season/time) to form the compound "மழைக்காலம்" (mazhaikkaalam, "rainy season"), where a hard க் sound is inserted at the join. Traditional grammar sorts these changes into categories such as உயிர்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (vowel-to-vowel sandhi), மெய்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (consonant-to-consonant sandhi) and உயிர்மெய்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (mixed sandhi). Recognising sandhi patterns helps you correctly split unfamiliar compound words back into their original parts when reading classical or formal Tamil.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.correctAnswer: The rules for combining words with sound changes at their junction

The formal structure of a letter
The meter used in classical poetry

tasks.content: Inbam Pal (இன்பத்துப்பால், also called காமத்துப்பால், Kaamathuppaal) is the third and final section of the Thirukkural, containing 250 couplets across 25 chapters devoted to the theme of இன்பம் (inbam, love). Unlike Aram Pal's ethical teachings or Porul Pal's public-life advice, this section is written as an intimate dialogue between a தலைவன் (thalaivan, hero/lover) and தலைவி (thalaivi, heroine/beloved), exploring courtship, longing, separation and reunion much like the akam poetry of the Sangam tradition. Its verses capture universal emotional experiences of romantic love — the shyness of first attraction, the ache of a lover's absence, the joy of reconciliation — in the same tightly structured two-line kural form used throughout the work. Studying Inbam Pal shows how classical Tamil literature treats love with the same careful craftsmanship as ethics and politics.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: The Jaffna Kingdom: Tamil History in Sri Lanka

tasks.taskName: Lesson: The Jaffna Kingdom: Tamil History in Sri Lanka
tasks.content: Tamil history is not only about mainland India — it also includes a long and proud history in இலங்கை (Sri Lanka). Around the 13th century CE, a Tamil kingdom known as the யாழ்ப்பாண இராச்சியம் (Jaffna Kingdom) was established in the northern part of Sri Lanka, ruled by the Aryacakravarti dynasty. Its capital was நல்லூர் (Nallur), which became an important center of Tamil Hindu (Saiva) culture, religion, and literature in the island. The kingdom built magnificent temples, most famously the நல்லூர் கந்தசுவாமி கோயில் (Nallur Kandaswamy Temple) dedicated to Lord Murugan, which remains one of the most important Hindu temples in Sri Lanka today. The Jaffna Kingdom traded with South India and other parts of the region, and its rulers supported Tamil scholars and poets, helping Tamil language and culture flourish in the north of the island for several centuries. The kingdom remained independent until 1619, when it was conquered by Portuguese colonizers — bringing an end to centuries of Tamil royal rule in Sri Lanka, though Tamil language, culture, and Hindu traditions continued to thrive among the Tamil community there.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This unit follows the central story of Silappathikaram in detail: Kannagi (கண்ணகி) and her husband Kovalan (கோவலன்) are a young married couple from Puhar, but Kovalan falls for a dancer named Madhavi (மாதவி) and squanders his fortune on her before returning, penniless, to Kannagi. The couple travels to Madurai to rebuild their lives, and Kannagi gives Kovalan her silambu (சிலம்பு, anklet) to sell — but he is wrongly accused of stealing the queen's anklet, which looks similar, and is unjustly executed by order of the Pandya king. Grief-stricken, Kannagi marches to the royal court and proves her husband's innocence by breaking open her remaining anklet: hers contains rubies, while the queen's contained pearls. In her fury at this injustice, Kannagi curses the city of Madurai, and this dramatic episode — Kannagi's grief turning to righteous anger — remains one of the most powerful moments in classical Tamil literature.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Kamba Ramayanam (கம்ப ராமாயணம்), also known as Ramavataram (இராமாவதாரம்), is the celebrated Tamil retelling of the Ramayana epic, composed by the poet Kambar (கம்பர்) around the 12th century CE. While it follows the same core story as Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana — Prince Rama's exile, the abduction of his wife Sita by the demon king Ravana, and the eventual war to rescue her — Kambar reshaped the narrative with rich Tamil poetic style, elaborate imagery and emotional depth suited to a Tamil audience of his era. The work is composed in thousands of verses across multiple kandams (books), and Kambar is often praised as one of the greatest poets in the Tamil literary tradition for the sheer craftsmanship of his verse. Kamba Ramayanam remains one of the most celebrated long narrative poems in Tamil literature, distinct in style and detail from its Sanskrit source.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Writing persuasively about a சமூகப் பிரச்சனை (samoogap pirachanai, social issue) means going beyond simple description to build an argument the reader can be convinced by. Choose a real topic such as சுற்றுச்சூழல் பாதுகாப்பு (environmental protection) or கல்வியின் முக்கியத்துவம் (the importance of education), then open with a clear thesis stating your position on it. Each body paragraph should present one piece of evidence or reasoning — a statistic, an example, or a logical argument — that directly supports that thesis, rather than simply listing loosely related facts. A strong persuasive essay on a social issue also briefly acknowledges an opposing view before explaining why your position remains stronger, which shows the reader you have thought the issue through carefully.

tasks.content: Building on the introduction to debate from Grade 6, this unit practises the formal roles and structure used in a organised Tamil வாதப் போட்டி (vaadhap potti, debate competition). Each side has a முன்மொழிபவர் (munmozhibavar, proposer) who opens the case, and speakers alternate presenting points within a strict கால வரம்பு (kaala varambu, time limit) enforced by a நடுவர் (naduvar, judge/adjudicator). A well-prepared formal debater doesn't just state opinions but organises them into a clear கட்டமைப்பு (kattamaippu, structure) — point, evidence, and a brief rebuttal of the opposing side's likely argument — delivered confidently within the time allowed. Practising this formal structure under timed conditions builds the confidence needed for real competitive debating.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Advanced translation goes beyond simple sentences to tackle idiomatic expressions, where a literal, word-for-word translation would sound strange or lose the original meaning entirely. For example, the Tamil proverb "கிணற்றுத் தவளைக்குக் கடல் தெரியுமா?" should not be translated literally as "does the well's frog know the ocean" but rendered with its equivalent English idiom, "like a frog in a well," to preserve the intended meaning for an English reader. Similarly, translating longer, more complex sentences requires reordering clauses — a Tamil sentence with a relative participle (பெயரெச்சம்) placed before a noun, like "நேற்று வந்த மாணவன்" (the student who came yesterday), must be restructured into an English relative clause with "who," since English cannot place a whole clause directly before a noun in the same way. Skilled translators balance staying faithful to the original meaning with producing natural, fluent sentences in the target language.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Puthukavithai (புதுக்கவிதை, "new poetry") is the modern free-verse movement in Tamil poetry that emerged in the 20th century as a deliberate break from the strict yaappu (poetic meter) rules that had shaped Tamil verse for centuries. Instead of fixed metrical patterns and rhyme, puthukavithai poets write in free verse, using natural rhythms of spoken Tamil, everyday vocabulary and contemporary themes — city life, personal emotion, social commentary — that older classical forms rarely addressed directly. This shift mirrors similar free-verse movements in other world literatures, where poets prioritised emotional directness and thematic freedom over rigid formal constraints. Reading puthukavithai alongside classical Sangam or Thirukkural verse highlights just how dramatically Tamil poetic form has evolved while the language itself remains continuous.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This review unit brings together the major strands of literature and composition studied across the year: the classical ethical wisdom of the Thirukkural, the ancient voice of Sangam poetry, the tragic grandeur of the Silappathikaram epic, and the modern freedom of puthukavithai. It also revisits composition skills built through essay writing on social issues, formal debate structure, and advanced translation between Tamil and English. Reviewing these topics together highlights how Tamil literature has continuously evolved in form — from strict classical meter to free modern verse — while composition and debate skills remain essential tools for expressing and defending ideas clearly, whether in an ancient couplet or a modern persuasive essay.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A formal Tamil letter (like to a school principal or government office) follows strict conventions: a respectful salutation, clear and polite language throughout, a formal closing like 'தங்கள் உண்மையுள்ள' (yours faithfully), and no casual or affectionate language. Getting the tone right in formal letters shows respect and makes your request or message more likely to be taken seriously.
Let's practice what we just learned!

What might a formal Tamil letter's closing phrase be?

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Tamil Grammar: Verb Conjugation Patterns
tasks.content: Tamil verbs follow patterns when conjugated (changed) for different tenses and subjects - recognising these patterns, rather than memorising every single form separately, makes learning verb forms much faster. For example, many verbs follow a similar shift between present ('-kiren' endings) and future ('-ven' endings) forms, once you know the base pattern.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does 'conjugating' a verb mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Changing it for different tenses and subjects
options: Changing it for different tenses and subjects

questions.questionText: What present-tense ending pattern is mentioned in this lesson?

questions.correctAnswer: once you know the base pattern, you can apply it to many different verbs

questions.questionText: What does recognising verb patterns help a learner do?
options: It only helps with nouns, not verbs

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: What changes on a Tamil verb to show a different tense, based on earlier lessons?

tasks.content: Analysing a Tamil short story means looking closely at its characters, setting, theme (the underlying message) and the writer's style - including word choice and how dialogue is used. Just as with English literature analysis, strong Tamil literary analysis supports its points with specific examples from the text, rather than vague general statements.
Let's practice what we just learned!

options: Only the title and author's name

questions.questionText: What does 'theme' mean in a short story?
What should strong literary analysis use to support its points?

Only guesses about the author's life

options: They follow a similar analytical approach

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: What should you avoid when making a literary analysis point, according to this lesson?

options: Setting can shape mood, context and the characters' circumstances

questions.questionText: What should support every analytical claim about a Tamil short story?

questions.questionText: Why might comparing Tamil and English analytical approaches be reassuring for a learner?

tasks.content: Studying extracts from Tamil literature means closely reading a short section of a larger work, paying attention to word choice, imagery, and the feelings or ideas the writer conveys. Even a short extract can reveal a lot about a writer's style and the themes of the whole piece, especially when read carefully more than once.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does studying a literature extract mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Closely reading a short section of a larger work
options: Closely reading a short section of a larger work

questions.questionText: Name one thing to pay attention to when studying an extract, mentioned in the lesson.
questions.correctAnswer: word choice (or imagery, or feelings/ideas conveyed)

questions.questionText: What can even a short extract reveal about the whole piece?
questions.correctAnswer: A writer's style and the themes of the whole piece
options: A writer's style and the themes of the whole piece
Only the page count of the book
Only the title of the chapter

questions.questionText: What is recommended to help understand an extract more deeply?
questions.correctAnswer: reading it carefully more than once

questions.questionText: Why might reading an extract more than once help with understanding it?
questions.correctAnswer: A first read gives overall meaning, while a second read reveals more detail and nuance
options: A first read gives overall meaning, while a second read reveals more detail and nuance
Rereading a text has no effect on understanding it
A single read always reveals every detail
Rereading only confuses the reader further

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

Extracts should always be analysed with no reference to the rest of the text
Broader context always makes analysis less accurate

questions.questionText: Why might comparing how two different Tamil writers use imagery in their extracts be a valuable exercise?

questions.questionText: Why does analysing literature extracts develop transferable reading skills?

Literature analysis has no connection to general reading ability

tasks.content: Tamil uses case markers (vetrumai urubu) attached to nouns to show their grammatical role in a sentence, similar to how English uses word order or prepositions. For example, adding '-ai' can mark an object (like 'puthagathai' - the book, as an object), while '-ukku' can show 'to/for' (like 'ammavukku' - to/for mother). These markers help clarify exactly how each noun relates to the action in a sentence.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What do case markers (vetrumai urubu) attach to?
What do case markers show about a noun in a sentence?
questions.correctAnswer: its grammatical role (how it relates to the action)

questions.questionText: What might the ending '-ai' mark on a noun, as mentioned in the lesson?
questions.correctAnswer: An object (like 'the book' as an object)
options: An object (like 'the book' as an object)

questions.questionText: What might the ending '-ukku' show, as mentioned in the lesson?
What does English typically use instead of case markers to show a similar grammatical role?
options: Nothing at all - English has no equivalent

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why might case markers be especially important in Tamil, which can have more flexible word order than English?
questions.correctAnswer: they clarify each noun's grammatical role even if the word order changes

questions.questionText: Why does comparing case markers to English prepositions help explain their function?
questions.correctAnswer: Both systems show how a noun relates to the rest of the sentence, just using different methods
options: Both systems show how a noun relates to the rest of the sentence, just using different methods
English prepositions and Tamil case markers have no similar function
Case markers only exist in Tamil, with no parallel concept elsewhere
Prepositions and case markers always work in opposite ways

questions.questionText: Why might 'ammavukku' (to/for mother) be used in a sentence about giving someone a gift?
questions.correctAnswer: the '-ukku' ending shows that the mother is the recipient (the person something is given to or for)

questions.questionText: Why is understanding case markers useful for correctly reading or writing Tamil sentences?
questions.correctAnswer: They show exactly how each noun functions, which is essential for understanding the sentence's full meaning
options: They show exactly how each noun functions, which is essential for understanding the sentence's full meaning
Case markers have no effect on a sentence's meaning
Only verbs matter for understanding a Tamil sentence
Case markers are optional and never affect meaning

questions.questionText: Why might a learner confuse the meaning of a sentence if they misunderstand a case marker ending?
questions.correctAnswer: the ending shows a noun's specific role, so misreading it could suggest the wrong relationship between words

questions.questionText: Why do linguists consider case-marking systems, like Tamil's vetrumai urubu, an efficient way to show grammar?
questions.correctAnswer: They let a single ending convey a grammatical role clearly, without needing strict word order
options: They let a single ending convey a grammatical role clearly, without needing strict word order
Case-marking systems are always less efficient than fixed word order
Case markers add unnecessary complexity with no benefit
Grammatical role can never be shown through word endings

tasks.content: Writing a speech in Tamil for an audience, such as for a school event, involves choosing a clear topic, using respectful and engaging language, and structuring the speech with an opening, main points, and a strong closing. Just like in English, pacing, tone and connecting with the audience's emotions are just as important as the words themselves.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What type of language should a speech use for its audience?

questions.correctAnswer: pacing, tone, and connecting with the audience's emotions

questions.questionText: What does this lesson say a Tamil speech has in common with an English speech?

The closing has no real importance in a speech

questions.correctAnswer: it helps them check their pacing, tone and timing, and become more comfortable with the content

questions.questionText: Why do speechwriting skills in Tamil and English share similar core principles?

tasks.content: A commentary ('urai') explains the meaning of a classical verse in detail, looking at word choice, context and deeper meaning. Writing a commentary involves close reading and explaining not just WHAT the verse says, but WHY it matters.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What is a commentary?
questions.correctAnswer: A detailed explanation of a verse's meaning
options: A detailed explanation of a verse's meaning

questions.questionText: What is the Tamil word for 'commentary'?
What does a commentary look at, besides the verse's basic meaning?
questions.correctAnswer: Word choice, context and deeper meaning
options: Word choice, context and deeper meaning

questions.questionText: Does a good commentary explain only WHAT a verse says, or also WHY it matters?
What reading skill does writing a commentary require?

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why might a classical verse need a commentary, rather than being immediately clear to a modern reader?

questions.questionText: Why does a commentary consider the HISTORICAL CONTEXT of a verse, not just its words?

questions.questionText: Why is studying classical commentary considered valuable for understanding Tamil literary tradition?

Classical commentary has no connection to literary tradition

Studying commentary has no educational value

tasks.content: Advertisements use persuasive language, like exaggeration, catchy slogans, and emotional appeals, to convince people to buy a product or believe an idea. Media literacy means being able to recognise these techniques rather than simply accepting messages at face value.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What is the goal of advertisement language?

options: To persuade people to buy a product or believe an idea

questions.questionText: Name one persuasive technique advertisements commonly use.
questions.correctAnswer: exaggeration, a catchy slogan, or an emotional appeal (any one)

questions.questionText: What does 'media literacy' mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Being able to recognise persuasive techniques in media
options: Being able to recognise persuasive techniques in media
Being unable to read any media at all
Believing everything you see in an advert

questions.questionText: Should you accept advertisement messages at face value, or think critically about them?

questions.questionText: Why is it important to question an advertisement's claims rather than accepting them immediately?

options: Advertisements are designed to persuade, so their claims may be exaggerated or one-sided

options: It helps students critically evaluate the persuasive messages that surround them daily, in Tamil and other languages

Advertisements should never be studied or analysed

tasks.content: A precis ('chourukkam') is a short summary of a longer text, written in your own words, that captures only the main ideas. A good precis is much shorter than the original but keeps its most important meaning.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What is a precis?
questions.correctAnswer: A short summary of a longer text
options: A short summary of a longer text
A long, detailed retelling with every detail

questions.questionText: What is the Tamil word for 'precis' used in this lesson?

Should a precis be written in the original author's exact words, or your own words?

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why is writing a precis in your OWN words, rather than copying the original, an important skill?
questions.correctAnswer: it shows you have understood the main ideas well enough to express them differently, not just memorised the wording

questions.questionText: Why should a precis avoid including minor details from the original text?
questions.correctAnswer: Minor details would make the precis longer and distract from capturing only the essential main ideas
options: Minor details would make the precis longer and distract from capturing only the essential main ideas
Minor details are always the most important part of a precis
A precis should always be longer than the original text
Every single detail must be included in a precis

questions.questionText: Why might writing a precis be a useful skill for exam revision?
questions.correctAnswer: condensing a long text into its main ideas helps you remember and review the key information more efficiently

questions.questionText: Why does a precis require strong reading comprehension before you can write one well?

options: You must first fully understand the original text to correctly identify which ideas are the most important
Precis writing requires no understanding of the original text at all

A precis can be written without reading the original text

questions.questionText: Why might a precis be useful when you need to share the key points of a long document with someone quickly?

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Functions in Python: Reusable Code
tasks.content: A function in Python is a named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task, similar to a procedure but with an important extra feature: a function can send a value back to whatever called it. A function is created using the def keyword, followed by a chosen name and round brackets, which may contain parameters, values passed into the function to use. For example: def greet(name): print("Hello, " + name) defines a function called greet that takes one parameter, name; calling greet("Amy") runs the indented code inside, printing Hello, Amy. Many functions also use the return keyword to send a result back, rather than just printing something directly. For example: def add(a, b): return a + b defines a function that calculates a sum and returns it; writing result = add(3, 4) then print(result) stores the returned value 7 in result and displays it. This matters because a returned value can be stored, compared, or used again elsewhere in the program, whereas something merely printed inside a function cannot be reused afterwards. If a function has no return statement, Python still gives it a result automatically: the special value None, meaning nothing was explicitly returned. Functions bring the same benefits as procedures, avoiding repeated code and making programs easier to read and test, but the ability to return values makes them especially powerful for calculations, since a function like square(n), returning n * n, can be reused anywhere a squared number is needed, keeping the main program short, clear, and focused on what should happen rather than exactly how each calculation is performed.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Lists and Data Structures in Python

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Lists and Data Structures in Python
tasks.content: A list is a data structure in Python used to store an ordered collection of items together in a single variable, rather than needing a separate variable for every value. A list is created using square brackets, with items separated by commas, for example fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"] creates a list of three strings. Each item in a list has a position, called an index, and Python indexing starts counting from 0, not 1, so fruits[0] refers to "apple", the first item, and fruits[1] refers to "banana". A negative index counts from the end of the list, so fruits[-1] refers to the last item, "cherry", which is useful when the exact length of a list is not known. The len() function returns how many items are in a list, so len(fruits) returns 3. Lists are mutable, meaning their contents can be changed after creation: nums = [10, 20, 30], then nums[1] = 99, changes the list to [10, 99, 30], replacing the item at index 1. New items can be added to the end of a list using the append() method, so fruits.append("date") changes the list to ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'date']. Lists work naturally with for loops, since for f in fruits: print(f) will run once for every item in the list, automatically printing each fruit on its own line without needing to know in advance how many items the list contains. Storing related data together in a list, rather than in many separate variables, makes programs far easier to manage, especially when the amount of data might grow or shrink while a program runs.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A string is a sequence of characters, and Python provides many built-in tools for examining and transforming strings, which is especially useful when working with user input or text data. Like a list, each character in a string has an index starting from 0, so for s = "Hello World", s[0] gives "H" and s[-1] gives the last character, "d". The len() function also works on strings, counting every character including spaces, so len(s) for "Hello World" returns 11. Strings have several useful built-in methods, called by adding a full stop after the string followed by the method name. The .upper() method returns a new version of the string in capital letters, so s.upper() returns "HELLO WORLD", while .lower() does the opposite, converting to lower case. The .split() method breaks a string into a list of smaller strings, dividing at a chosen character, most often a space; s.split(" ") on "Hello World" returns the list ["Hello", "World"], which is very useful for processing sentences word by word. The .replace() method searches for one piece of text within a string and swaps it for another, so s.replace("World", "Python") returns "Hello Python", leaving the original string in s unchanged unless the result is stored back into a variable. Strings can also be joined together, or concatenated, using the plus sign, so "Hello" + " " + "World" produces "Hello World". It is important to remember that these methods do not change the original string in place; Python strings are immutable, so each method call produces a brand new string, which must be stored in a variable if it needs to be kept and used later.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Boolean Logic and Truth Tables
tasks.content: Boolean logic deals with values that can only be True or False, and it underlies every decision a computer makes, from a simple if statement to the design of the circuits inside a CPU. Three fundamental logical operators combine or change these values: AND, OR and NOT. The AND operator produces True only when both of its inputs are True; in Python, True and False evaluates to False, since one input is False. The OR operator produces True when at least one of its inputs is True; True or False evaluates to True, because at least one side is True. The NOT operator simply reverses a single value; not True evaluates to False, and not False evaluates to True. A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs and shows the resulting output, which is a clear way to fully describe how a logical operator behaves. For AND, with inputs A and B, the table shows: 0 and 0 gives 0, 0 and 1 gives 0, 1 and 0 gives 0, and only 1 and 1 gives 1, using 1 for True and 0 for False. For OR, the table shows: 0 or 0 gives 0, but 0 or 1, 1 or 0, and 1 or 1 all give 1, since only one input needs to be True. These simple rules are combined to build more complex conditions in programs, such as checking that a password is both long enough and contains a number, which would use AND, or checking that a user is either an administrator or a verified member, which would use OR. The same logic gates, built from electronic circuits, are also the basic building blocks used inside a CPU to perform arithmetic and make decisions at the hardware level.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Representing Text, Images and Sound in Binary

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Representing Text, Images and Sound in Binary
tasks.content: Every type of data a computer handles, whatever it looks or sounds like to a human, is ultimately stored as patterns of binary digits, using agreed coding systems that both the computer and its software understand. Text is represented using character sets, which assign a unique binary code to every letter, digit and symbol. The older ASCII system uses patterns of bits to represent English letters, digits and basic punctuation, so, for example, the capital letter 'A' is represented by the denary value 65, which is 01000001 in binary; because it only supports a limited number of characters, modern systems increasingly use Unicode instead, which uses more bits to represent a vastly larger range of characters, including accented letters, non-Latin alphabets and emoji, from many of the world's languages. Images are represented as a grid of tiny coloured squares called pixels; the more pixels used, called the resolution, the more detailed the image can be. Each pixel's colour is itself stored in binary, commonly using 8 bits for each of red, green and blue, called colour depth, giving 24 bits per pixel and allowing over 16 million possible colours; higher resolution and greater colour depth both produce better quality images but also significantly larger file sizes. Sound is represented by sampling: a microphone or sound wave is measured, and its amplitude at each moment is recorded as a binary number, many times every second. The sample rate is how many samples are taken per second, and the sample resolution, or bit depth, is how many bits are used to store each sample; increasing either produces a more accurate recreation of the original sound but also increases the file size considerably.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: How the CPU Executes Instructions
tasks.content: The central processing unit constantly repeats a process called the fetch-decode-execute cycle in order to run every program, from a simple calculator app to a full operating system. First, in the fetch stage, the CPU retrieves the next instruction from memory, using a special register called the Program Counter to keep track of which instruction should be fetched next, and the Memory Address Register and Memory Data Register to locate and collect that instruction from RAM. Next, in the decode stage, the instruction is translated so the CPU understands exactly what operation it represents and what data, if any, it needs. Finally, in the execute stage, the CPU actually carries out the instruction, which might involve a calculation, moving data, or making a decision, often using a register called the Accumulator to store the result. This entire cycle then repeats for the next instruction, happening billions of times every second in a modern computer. The speed at which this cycle repeats is measured by the clock speed, given in Hertz (Hz), or more commonly gigahertz (GHz) for modern processors, where one gigahertz means one billion cycles per second; a higher clock speed generally allows more instructions to be processed every second, making the computer perform tasks faster, although it is not the only factor affecting performance. Many modern CPUs also contain multiple cores, essentially several separate processing units built into a single chip, allowing genuinely different tasks, or parts of the same task, to be worked on at the same time, called parallel processing. CPUs also use a small amount of extremely fast memory called cache, positioned very close to the processor, to store frequently used data and instructions so they can be accessed far more quickly than fetching the same information from RAM every single time.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: The Internet: Protocols and the World Wide Web

tasks.taskName: Lesson: The Internet: Protocols and the World Wide Web
tasks.content: Although the terms are often used interchangeably, the internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing. The internet is the huge, physical network of networks connecting devices worldwide, while the World Wide Web is a service that runs on top of the internet, made up of linked web pages and websites accessed through a browser; email, online gaming and video calls also run over the internet but are not part of the Web itself. For all these services to work reliably, devices must agree on protocols, which are sets of rules that define exactly how data should be formatted, sent and received, so that different devices and software, even from different manufacturers, can communicate successfully. The Transmission Control Protocol, or TCP, is responsible for breaking data into packets before sending, checking that every packet arrives correctly, and reassembling them in the right order at the destination, requesting any missing packets again if needed. The Internet Protocol, or IP, works alongside TCP, handling addressing and making sure each packet is routed toward the correct destination device based on its IP address; together these are often referred to as TCP/IP. For browsing the Web specifically, the HyperText Transfer Protocol, or HTTP, defines how a browser requests a web page and how a server responds with that page's content; HTTPS is a more secure version of the same protocol, encrypting the data exchanged so that anyone intercepting it cannot easily read it, which is essential whenever sensitive information, such as passwords or payment details, is being sent. Other protocols handle other tasks, such as FTP for transferring files between computers, showing that the smooth operation of the internet actually depends on many different, carefully agreed protocols working correctly together.
Let's practice what we just learned!
