tasks.content: Sorting algorithms arrange data in order - bubble sort repeatedly compares and swaps neighbouring items until the list is sorted, which is simple but slow for large lists. Searching algorithms find an item within data - linear search checks each item one by one, while binary search (on already-sorted data) repeatedly halves the search area, finding items much faster.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does a sorting algorithm do?
What sorting algorithm repeatedly compares and swaps neighbouring items?
What is a downside of bubble sort?
questions.correctAnswer: It is slow for large lists
options: It is slow for large lists

questions.questionText: What searching algorithm checks each item one by one?
What must be true about data before you can use binary search on it?

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: How does binary search find items faster than linear search?
questions.correctAnswer: by repeatedly halving the search area

questions.questionText: Why is binary search generally faster than linear search on sorted data?
questions.correctAnswer: It eliminates half the remaining data with each comparison
options: It checks every single item, just like linear search
It eliminates half the remaining data with each comparison
Binary search is always slower than linear search
Binary search only works on unsorted data

questions.questionText: What is a 'searching algorithm' used to do, as opposed to a sorting algorithm?
questions.correctAnswer: find a specific item within data

questions.questionText: Which algorithm would be more efficient for searching a very large, already-sorted list?
Why might bubble sort still be taught, despite being slow for large lists?
questions.correctAnswer: it's simple to understand and a good introduction to sorting concepts

questions.questionText: Which best summarises the difference between sorting and searching algorithms?
questions.correctAnswer: Sorting arranges data in order; searching finds specific items within it
options: They are exactly the same type of algorithm
Sorting arranges data in order; searching finds specific items within it
Sorting finds items; searching arranges them
Neither has a clear distinct purpose

levels.moduleName: Module 5: Advanced Python Projects & Exam Skills

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Coding Exam Technique & Final Project
tasks.content: Strong coding exam technique means reading questions carefully to know exactly what a program must do, planning your logic (with pseudocode or a flowchart) before writing code, testing thoroughly with a range of inputs, and checking your code against the question's exact requirements before finishing. A strong final project reflects everything learned: clear planning, working code, and careful testing.

questions.questionText: What should you do carefully first with a coding exam question?

Start typing code immediately with no reading

questions.questionText: What should you check your finished code against, before submitting?
What does a strong final project reflect?

options: Clear planning, working code, and careful testing

questions.questionText: Why is planning with pseudocode valuable before writing exam code under time pressure?

questions.questionText: Why should you test your code with a range of inputs, not just one?

Testing has no value in exams

questions.questionText: What final check should you do before considering an exam coding task complete?

questions.questionText: Which best reflects strong overall coding exam technique?

options: Writing code with no plan or testing

tasks.content: A class is a blueprint for creating objects, defining what data (attributes) and actions (methods) they have - like class Dog: with attributes name and breed, and a method bark(). An object is a specific instance created from that class, like my_dog = Dog("Rex", "Labrador"), giving you a real dog object with its own specific name and breed.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What is a class?
What is an object, in relation to a class?
questions.correctAnswer: a specific instance created from that class

questions.questionText: In 'class Dog: name, breed, bark()', what are 'name' and 'breed'?
In the same example, what is 'bark()'?
What does 'my_dog = Dog("Rex", "Labrador")' create?
questions.correctAnswer: An object (a specific dog instance) with its own name and breed
options: An object (a specific dog instance) with its own name and breed

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: If you created another_dog = Dog("Milo", "Poodle"), would it share the exact same name as my_dog?
questions.correctAnswer: no, each object instance has its own separate attribute values

questions.questionText: Which best describes the relationship between a class and its objects?
questions.correctAnswer: A class is a blueprint; objects are specific instances built from that blueprint
options: A class is a blueprint; objects are specific instances built from that blueprint
A class and an object are always identical
Objects are blueprints; classes are instances
Classes cannot create more than one object

questions.questionText: Why might object-oriented programming organise related data and actions together in a class?
questions.correctAnswer: it keeps related attributes and methods logically grouped and easier to manage

questions.questionText: Why might a game use classes for characters, like 'Player' and 'Enemy'?
questions.correctAnswer: Each character type can share a consistent structure while having its own specific data
options: Each character type can share a consistent structure while having its own specific data
Classes have no use in game character design
Every character must use entirely separate, unrelated code
Classes only work for animals, not game characters

questions.questionText: What do we call the specific data values and actions a class defines, together?

questions.correctAnswer: A class defines a reusable structure; objects are individual instances built from it, each with their own data
options: A class defines a reusable structure; objects are individual instances built from it, each with their own data
Classes and objects are unrelated programming concepts
Only one object can ever be created from a class
Objects define classes, not the other way around

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Big O Notation & Efficiency Basics
tasks.content: Big O notation is a way to describe how an algorithm's run time grows as the amount of data increases, like O(n) meaning time grows directly with the data size (checking every item once), or O(n^2) meaning time grows much faster (like comparing every item to every other item). Understanding efficiency helps programmers choose better algorithms for large amounts of data.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does Big O notation describe?
questions.correctAnswer: How an algorithm's run time grows as data increases
options: How an algorithm's run time grows as data increases
The exact colour of a program's output
The file size of a program

questions.questionText: What does O(n) typically mean?
questions.correctAnswer: time grows directly with the data size (e.g. checking every item once)

questions.questionText: What does O(n^2) typically mean, compared to O(n)?
questions.correctAnswer: Time grows much faster, like comparing every item to every other item
options: Time grows much faster, like comparing every item to every other item
Time grows at exactly the same rate as O(n)
The algorithm always runs instantly regardless of data size

questions.questionText: Why is understanding algorithm efficiency useful for programmers?
questions.correctAnswer: it helps them choose better algorithms for large amounts of data

questions.questionText: Which algorithm would likely run faster on very large data: one with O(n) or O(n^2)?
options: They are always exactly the same speed

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why might an O(n^2) algorithm become a problem with very large amounts of data?
questions.correctAnswer: its run time grows much faster than the data size, becoming very slow for big inputs

questions.questionText: Which best shows an O(n) process?
questions.correctAnswer: Checking every item in a list exactly once
options: Checking every item in a list exactly once
Comparing every item in a list to every other item
Running a fixed number of steps no matter the data size
Doing nothing at all with the data

questions.questionText: Why might comparing 'every item to every other item' (as in O(n^2)) take much longer than checking each item once?
questions.correctAnswer: the number of comparisons grows much faster as the data size increases, compared to a single pass

questions.questionText: Why is Big O notation useful even without running the actual code?
questions.correctAnswer: It allows programmers to reason about and compare algorithm efficiency theoretically
options: It allows programmers to reason about and compare algorithm efficiency theoretically
Big O notation requires running the code every time to have any meaning
Efficiency can never be estimated without running a program
Big O notation has no real use for programmers

questions.questionText: What happens to an algorithm's run time if its efficiency is described as O(n) and the data doubles?
questions.correctAnswer: the run time roughly doubles as well

questions.questionText: Which best summarises the purpose of learning Big O notation at this level?
questions.correctAnswer: Understanding how to measure and compare algorithm efficiency as data grows
options: Understanding how to measure and compare algorithm efficiency as data grows
Big O notation only describes a program's appearance, not its speed
Efficiency has no connection to how algorithms are chosen
All algorithms run at exactly the same speed regardless of notation

levels.levelName: Final Capstone: Planning a Multi-Feature Program

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Final Capstone: Planning a Multi-Feature Program
tasks.content: As a final capstone project, planning a multi-feature program means combining everything learned: classes for organising data, functions for reusable logic, loops and conditionals for control flow, and testing to check it all works. Capstone projects introduce entirely new, unrelated skills

tasks.content: Inheritance lets a new class (a 'child' class) be based on an existing class (a 'parent' class), inheriting its attributes and methods while adding or changing some of its own - like a 'Dog' class inheriting from a general 'Animal' class. Polymorphism lets different classes share the same method name but behave differently, like each animal class having its own 'make_sound' method.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does inheritance let a new class do?
questions.correctAnswer: Be based on an existing class, inheriting its attributes and methods
options: Be based on an existing class, inheriting its attributes and methods
Create a completely unrelated class with no connection

questions.questionText: What is the class being inherited FROM usually called?
What is the new class that inherits from another usually called?
What does polymorphism let different classes share, while behaving differently?
What example of polymorphism is given in the lesson?
questions.correctAnswer: Each animal class having its own 'make_sound' method
options: Each animal class having its own 'make_sound' method
Every class having an identical, unchangeable method
Classes that can never share any method names
A single class with no methods at all

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why might a 'Dog' class inheriting from an 'Animal' class save time, compared to writing Dog's code completely from scratch?
questions.correctAnswer: the Dog class can automatically reuse any shared attributes and methods already defined in the Animal class, only needing to add or change what's specific to dogs

questions.questionText: Why is inheritance useful for organising related classes, like Dog, Cat and Bird, that share common animal characteristics?
questions.correctAnswer: It lets shared features be defined once in a parent class, while each child class adds only its own specific differences
options: It lets shared features be defined once in a parent class, while each child class adds only its own specific differences
Inheritance provides no real benefit for organising related classes
Every related class must always be written completely independently, with no shared code

questions.questionText: Why might each animal class need its own version of a 'make_sound' method, rather than sharing exactly one identical method?
questions.correctAnswer: different animals make different sounds, so each class needs its own specific version of the method to produce the correct, appropriate behaviour

questions.questionText: Why is polymorphism useful if you want to call 'make_sound()' on a list of different animal objects, without checking each one's exact type first?
questions.correctAnswer: Polymorphism lets you call the same method name on each object, and each one automatically runs its own correct version, without needing extra checks
options: Polymorphism lets you call the same method name on each object, and each one automatically runs its own correct version, without needing extra checks
You would always need to manually check each object's type before calling any method
Polymorphism has no real benefit for working with different types of objects
Calling the same method name on different objects always causes an error

questions.questionText: Why might a child class 'override' (change) a method it inherited from its parent class, rather than keeping the exact same version?
questions.correctAnswer: the child class might need slightly different, more specific behaviour than the general version provided by the parent class

questions.questionText: Why are inheritance and polymorphism considered advanced but powerful object-oriented programming concepts?
questions.correctAnswer: They let programmers organise and reuse code efficiently while still allowing flexibility for different, related types of objects to behave appropriately
options: They let programmers organise and reuse code efficiently while still allowing flexibility for different, related types of objects to behave appropriately
These concepts have no real benefit for organising object-oriented code
Inheritance and polymorphism are never actually used in real programming
This is considered a completely unimportant area of object-oriented programming

tasks.content: An API (Application Programming Interface) lets different programs communicate with each other, often used to get data from the internet, like current weather information, in a structured format (commonly JSON). Using an API usually involves sending a request to a specific address (URL) and receiving a structured response back to use in your program.
Let's practice what we just learned!

questions.questionText: What does an API let different programs do?
options: Only display the exact same picture

questions.questionText: What does API stand for?
What is an API often used to get, according to the lesson's example?
options: Only a single fixed number, never real data
Only images with no other data

questions.questionText: What common structured format is used for API data, mentioned in the lesson?
What does using an API usually involve, according to the lesson?
questions.correctAnswer: Sending a request to a specific address (URL) and receiving a structured response
options: Sending a request to a specific address (URL) and receiving a structured response
Nothing at all - APIs require no request or response
Only deleting files, with no data exchange
Writing a letter and mailing it physically

tasks.content: Time to show what you know!

questions.questionText: Why might a weather app use an API, rather than trying to collect weather data itself?
questions.correctAnswer: an API lets it access data already collected and maintained by another specialised service, saving enormous effort compared to gathering that data independently

questions.questionText: Why is a structured data format like JSON useful for an API's response?
questions.correctAnswer: It organises the returned data in a predictable, consistent way that programs can reliably read and process
options: It organises the returned data in a predictable, consistent way that programs can reliably read and process
JSON makes API responses completely impossible for programs to understand

questions.questionText: Why does using an API typically require sending a request to a specific URL?
questions.correctAnswer: the URL identifies exactly where and what resource or data is being requested from the API provider's system

questions.questionText: Why might many different apps and websites rely on the same weather API, rather than each building their own weather data collection system?
questions.correctAnswer: Reusing a shared, reliable API is often more practical and efficient than every single app duplicating the same complex data-gathering effort independently
options: Reusing a shared, reliable API is often more practical and efficient than every single app duplicating the same complex data-gathering effort independently
Every single app must always build its own completely separate data collection system
Sharing a common API provides no advantage over building independent systems

questions.questionText: Why might a program need to convert an API's JSON response into Python data structures, like dictionaries or lists, to use the information?

questions.questionText: Why is learning the basics of working with APIs considered a valuable, practical programming skill?

options: Many real-world applications rely on APIs to access shared data and services, making this a widely applicable and useful skill
APIs have no real connection to how real-world applications actually work

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Final Capstone: a Multi-Feature Program
tasks.content: A capstone project brings together everything learned throughout the Coding modules: variables, loops, conditions, functions, data structures, and classes, combined into one complete, multi-feature program, like a text-based adventure game with an inventory system, multiple rooms, and a simple save/load feature using file handling.

questions.questionText: Why might a text-based adventure game be a good choice for a final capstone project, combining so many different skills?

questions.questionText: Why might using classes to represent rooms or items in an adventure game be more organised than using many separate, unconnected variables?

questions.questionText: Why is a capstone project considered a valuable way to demonstrate everything learned across the Coding modules, rather than testing each skill separately?

questions.questionText: Why might planning the structure of a multi-feature program, like this adventure game, before coding be especially important?

questions.questionText: Why does completing a capstone project like this mark a meaningful milestone in a student's coding journey through this subject?
